note: Derived from the mechanisms on these cards and checked against FDA labeling where a claim was uncertain. It covers the interactions a fundamentals exam asks about and a nurse should recognize at the bedside. It is NOT a complete interaction screen and does not replace a pharmacy check or an interaction database.

severity_key.avoid: Do not combine without a specific, deliberate reason.
severity_key.high: Combine only with active monitoring; this is where patients get hurt.
severity_key.moderate: Usually manageable with timing, dose adjustment, or closer watching.

rules.name: Bleeding risk stacks
rules.mechanism:
Stopping a bleed takes two steps. Platelets clump together to form a plug, then a mesh of fibrin locks that plug in place. These drugs attack different steps.

Anticoagulants stop the fibrin mesh. Antiplatelets stop the plug. NSAIDs do two things at once by blocking COX-1: they weaken platelets AND strip the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, so you get worse clotting and a surface more likely to bleed. SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need in order to clump.

Combine any two and the risk compounds. Some of these pairs are closer to additive than multiplied, but none of them are safe to stack without watching for it.
rules.watch: Bruising, gum and nose bleeding, hematuria, tarry stool, new or worsening headache. H&H and platelets.
rules.exam: Two anticoagulants together is almost always wrong, EXCEPT a deliberate bridge: heparin or enoxaparin overlapping warfarin until the INR is therapeutic, or the 5-day parenteral lead-in dabigatran requires. Know the difference between a bridge and a duplication.

rules.name: Potassium climbs
rules.mechanism: ACE inhibitors and ARBs remove aldosterone, so the kidney stops dumping K⁺. Trimethoprim blocks the distal tubule sodium channel directly, which is structurally how amiloride works. Heparin and enoxaparin suppress aldosterone synthesis in the adrenal gland, independent of their anticoagulant effect.
rules.watch: Serum K⁺. ECG for peaked T waves, widening QRS, lost P waves. Muscle weakness.
rules.exam: Lisinopril plus Bactrim is the classic tested pair and a real cause of hospitalization. Hyperkalemia flattens the resting membrane potential until sodium channels can't reset, so the heart slows, blocks, and arrests.

rules.name: Potassium falls
rules.mechanism: Loop diuretics dump K⁺ at the loop of Henle. Prednisone and methylprednisolone hold Na⁺ and trade away K⁺ through mineralocorticoid activity. Dexamethasone has almost none of that activity, so its hypokalemia is weaker and arrives by other routes at high dose. Insulin and sodium bicarbonate don't remove potassium at all, they drive it into cells, which looks identical on a lab draw.
rules.watch: K⁺ and Mg²⁺ together, because you cannot correct potassium while magnesium is low. ECG for U waves and ectopy.
rules.exam: This rule feeds the QT rule. Low K⁺ and low Mg²⁺ lengthen the QT on their own, so a patient on furosemide who then gets ondansetron is at far more torsades risk than either drug suggests alone.

rules.name: QT prolongation and torsades
rules.mechanism:
After each beat the ventricle has to repolarize, meaning reset its electrical charge, before it can beat again. Potassium leaving the cell through the hERG channel is what does that. These drugs block hERG, so repolarization drags out. That dragged-out reset is what a long QT measures, and a beat firing during that stretched window can tip the rhythm into torsades de pointes.

They do not all carry the same weight. Ondansetron, methadone, prochlorperazine, chlorpromazine, haloperidol, amitriptyline, the fluoroquinolones and the macrolides, Bactrim, and the antiarrhythmics amiodarone and procainamide are the established ones. Loperamide belongs here only at HIGHER THAN RECOMMENDED doses, which is what its boxed warning is about. Loperamide belongs here only at HIGHER THAN RECOMMENDED doses, which is what its boxed warning is about. For the antiarrhythmics the QT effect IS the mechanism, not a side effect, which is why a class IA or class III drug can treat an arrhythmia and cause torsades with the same action. Escitalopram, quetiapine and olanzapine prolong QT only modestly (escitalopram by about 7 msec at 20 mg), and for metronidazole the evidence is case reports while fluoxetine's effect is marginal, so treat all of those as a reason to check rather than a reason to expect it.

The SSRI with a genuinely QT-driven dose restriction is CITALOPRAM, not escitalopram.
rules.watch: Baseline and follow-up ECG. Correct K⁺ and Mg²⁺ BEFORE giving, because correcting them is what actually lowers the risk.
rules.exam: Metronidazole's own label names the interaction: QT prolongation reported 'particularly when administered with drugs with the potential for prolonging the QT interval.' The common hospital version is a patient on furosemide receiving ondansetron plus a fluoroquinolone.

rules.name: Sedation and respiratory depression
rules.mechanism: Opioids blunt the brainstem's response to rising CO₂. Benzodiazepines amplify GABA. Gabapentinoids damp excitatory transmission. Stacked, the drive to breathe can disappear while the patient simply looks asleep.
rules.watch: Respiratory rate and sedation level before AND after every dose. Sedation rises before the rate falls, so a rousable-but-drowsy patient is the warning, not the reassurance. Naloxone available.
rules.exam: Opioid plus benzodiazepine carries a black box on both drugs. Opioid plus gabapentinoid carries an FDA warning added in 2019. If a question hands you a patient on an opioid and lorazepam, respiratory status is the answer.

rules.name: Serotonin syndrome
rules.mechanism:
Too much serotonin at the synapse. The SSRIs and SNRIs here (fluoxetine, sertraline, escitalopram, venlafaxine, duloxetine) raise it directly by blocking its reuptake. Amitriptyline does the same, alongside norepinephrine. Methadone and buspirone contribute weakly.

Ondansetron and metoclopramide are a different case. They BLOCK serotonin receptors rather than raising serotonin, and the link to serotonin syndrome rests on case reports with no established mechanism. Treat them as a reason to look, not a reason to expect it.
rules.watch: Agitation, hyperthermia, tachycardia, labile BP, HYPERREFLEXIA and clonus, diarrhea.
rules.exam: Hyperreflexia and clonus separate serotonin syndrome from NMS, which has lead-pipe rigidity and hyporeflexia. Onset is hours, not days. A post-op patient on duloxetine who gets ondansetron is the realistic scenario.

rules.name: Acute kidney injury (the triple whammy)
rules.mechanism:
The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

CYCLOSPORINE belongs to the first mechanism rather than the third: its acute nephrotoxicity is AFFERENT arteriolar vasoconstriction, the same vessel an NSAID narrows, which is why cyclosporine plus an NSAID is worse than simply additive.

Gentamicin and vancomycin skip all of that and injure the tubule itself, so they add to any of the three. IV acyclovir is a third kind: it crystallizes inside the tubule when the urine is concentrated, which makes it a hydration problem rather than a dose problem, and it applies to the IV route only.

An NSAID blocks the prostaglandins, so the afferent arteriole narrows and less blood gets in. An ACE inhibitor or ARB blocks angiotensin II, so the efferent arteriole relaxes open and pressure escapes. A diuretic drops the volume arriving at both. Take all three and filtration pressure collapses.
rules.watch: BUN, creatinine, eGFR, urine output, daily weight.
rules.exam: 'Triple whammy' is the actual name in the literature. It is one of the most common preventable causes of hospital-acquired AKI, and all three drugs are things a patient may already be taking for good reasons.

rules.name: Bradycardia and AV block
rules.mechanism:
Beta blockers slow the SA and AV node through the sympathetic pathway. Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers slow the same nodes through calcium entry. Two different doors into the same room.

Amiodarone, digoxin and lacosamide reach the same nodes by three more routes. Most of these combinations are deliberate rate control rather than errors, so the question is almost never whether to allow the pair but what hold parameter is written and whether anyone looked at an ECG. The one pairing that genuinely stands out is a beta blocker with diltiazem or verapamil.
rules.watch: Apical pulse for a full minute, BP, ECG for PR interval and dropped beats.
rules.exam: Amlodipine is the safe CCB here, because it is vessel-selective and does nothing to the AV node. Verapamil is the most dangerous of the pair, and IV verapamil with an IV beta blocker can cause asystole.

rules.name: CYP3A4 inhibition raises drug levels
rules.mechanism:
These inhibitors block the enzyme that clears the substrates, so the substrate accumulates at an unchanged dose. CYCLOSPORINE is in both roles: it inhibits CYP3A4 and OATP1B1, and it is itself a 3A4 substrate, so its level swings with anything that touches the enzyme and it raises the levels of others. CYCLOSPORINE is in both roles: it inhibits CYP3A4 and OATP1B1, and it is itself a 3A4 substrate, so its level swings with anything that touches the enzyme and it raises the levels of others. CYCLOSPORINE is in both roles: it inhibits CYP3A4 and OATP1B1, and it is itself a 3A4 substrate, so its level swings with anything that touches the enzyme and it raises the levels of others. CYCLOSPORINE is in both roles: it inhibits CYP3A4 and OATP1B1, and it is itself a 3A4 substrate, so its level swings with anything that touches the enzyme and it raises the levels of others.

Erythromycin is a POTENT inhibitor and the strongest in this set; diltiazem and verapamil are moderate. Amlodipine is a WEAK inhibitor and is not listed here: its one labeled consequence is the simvastatin 20 mg cap, which is carried as a named pair instead.
rules.watch: Statin: new muscle pain, weakness, dark urine, CK. DOAC: any bleeding.
rules.exam: Diltiazem or verapamil with simvastatin is the textbook pair, and the simvastatin dose is capped at 10 mg because of it. Grapefruit juice belongs in the same bucket.

rules.name: CYP2D6 inhibition by fluoxetine
rules.mechanism: Fluoxetine, PAROXETINE and bupropion are all potent CYP2D6 inhibitors. The fluoxetine metabolite norfluoxetine has a 4-16 day half-life, so the blockade persists for WEEKS after fluoxetine is stopped. For a drug cleared by 2D6, the level climbs. For a PRODRUG that needs 2D6 to be activated, the opposite happens: it never converts, so it stops working.
rules.watch: Pain relief that never arrives; or unexpected bradycardia.
rules.exam: This is the one interaction that makes a drug fail rather than overdose. Easy to miss because nothing looks wrong on the monitor.

rules.name: Enzyme inducers strip other drugs
rules.mechanism:
Phenytoin, CARBAMAZEPINE and RIFAMPIN are all strong inducers of CYP enzymes and P-glycoprotein. They accelerate the clearance of a long list of drugs, so those drugs drop below therapeutic levels at an unchanged dose.

Get the DIRECTION right, because it is the whole concept and it is the thing students reverse. An inducer makes the other drug WEAKER. An inhibitor makes it STRONGER. With an inducer the danger is treatment failure: a clot, a seizure, a pregnancy, a rejected transplant. With an inhibitor the danger is toxicity. Induction also builds over one to two weeks and takes weeks to wear off, so the interaction outlasts the drug.
rules.watch: Drug levels for phenytoin and valproate, INR for warfarin, and signs the other drug has simply stopped working.
rules.exam: The valproate-phenytoin pair is the subtle one. Nystagmus and ataxia in a patient whose total phenytoin level is 'fine' means check a FREE level and check albumin.

rules.name: Antibiotics push the INR up
rules.mechanism:
Two routes. All of them kill the gut bacteria that make vitamin K, which is the vitamin warfarin already works against, so the warfarin effect deepens. Metronidazole, Bactrim, erythromycin and isoniazid do something extra: they also block the enzyme that clears warfarin, so the drug itself builds up. Two hits instead of one is why those push the INR hardest.

RIFAMPIN is the exception that reverses the whole rule. It INDUCES the enzyme instead of blocking it, so the INR FALLS and the patient clots while looking anticoagulated on paper. See the induction rule.
rules.watch: Recheck INR within a few days of starting OR stopping the antibiotic. Stopping it swings the INR back down.
rules.exam: Metronidazole and Bactrim are the two that spike the INR hardest. Any new antibiotic in a warfarin patient means an INR recheck, not a wait-and-see.

rules.name: Binders and cations block absorption
rules.mechanism: Divalent and trivalent cations chelate fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines in the gut, forming a complex that is never absorbed. Sevelamer is a polymer that binds far more than phosphate. Raising gastric pH changes absorption of drugs that need acid.
rules.watch: Treatment failure. The antibiotic level never gets high enough to work and nothing looks wrong at the bedside.
rules.exam: Separate by 2-6 hr. Sevelamer specifically: give other oral drugs 1 hr before or 3 hr after. This is a timing problem, not a do-not-combine problem.

rules.name: Dopamine blockers stack (EPS, NMS)
rules.mechanism:
All of these block central D2 receptors. Stack two and the blockade deepens, and so does every consequence of it: extrapyramidal symptoms, akathisia, tardive dyskinesia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

The pairing that gets missed is an antipsychotic patient who is then given metoclopramide or prochlorperazine for nausea. Ondansetron does not block dopamine and is the safer antiemetic in that patient.
rules.watch: Akathisia, acute dystonia, parkinsonian features, tardive dyskinesia, and NMS (fever, lead-pipe rigidity, altered consciousness).
rules.exam: Akathisia gets mistaken for untreated nausea or anxiety, so the reflex is to give MORE antiemetic, which makes it worse. Treat acute dystonia with diphenhydramine or benztropine.

rules.name: GI ulceration and bleeding
rules.mechanism: NSAIDs remove the prostaglandins that protect gastric mucosa. Steroids impair mucosal healing and mask the pain that would warn you. SSRIs add impaired platelet function on top.
rules.watch: Black or tarry stool, coffee-ground emesis, epigastric pain, falling H&H.
rules.exam: The steroid is what makes this dangerous, because it removes the warning pain. A patient on prednisone and ibuprofen can perforate without ever complaining of their stomach.

rules.name: NSAIDs blunt blood pressure drugs
rules.mechanism: Antihypertensives and diuretics rely partly on prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation and renal sodium handling. NSAIDs block prostaglandin synthesis, so the BP drug works less well and sodium is retained.
rules.watch: BP creeping up, new edema, weight gain, a diuretic that stopped working.
rules.exam: If a question gives you a patient whose controlled BP suddenly isn't, look for a new over-the-counter NSAID before you look for nonadherence.

rules.name: Glucose control gets pushed both ways
rules.mechanism: Steroids drive gluconeogenesis and reduce peripheral glucose uptake, so insulin requirements rise, sometimes steeply. Beta blockers do something different and more dangerous: they mask the adrenergic warning signs of hypoglycemia (tremor, tachycardia) while sweating still comes through.
rules.watch: More frequent glucose checks. On a beta blocker, treat diaphoresis as hypoglycemia until proven otherwise.
rules.exam: Propranolol is the worst of the four, because nonselective blockade also blunts the glycogenolysis that would self-correct the low.

rules.name: Drugs that work against each other
rules.mechanism: Direct pharmacologic antagonism. One drug undoes what the other is for.
rules.watch: Ask why both are ordered. This is usually a reconciliation error rather than a plan.
rules.exam: Tranexamic acid is the only drug in this whole set whose job is to KEEP clot. Every anticoagulant and antiplatelet is its opposite.

rules.name: Muscle injury and rhabdomyolysis
rules.mechanism:
Statins, fibrates and niacin each injure muscle on their own, and together the risk climbs. Muscle pain and weakness are the warning. Rhabdomyolysis is the endpoint: muscle breaking down fast enough to damage the kidneys.

Why this is moderate and not high: the fibrate behind the serious cases is GEMFIBROZIL, which slows how fast the body clears a statin, so the statin builds up. Fenofibrate does not do that, which is exactly why it is the fibrate you pair with a statin. Gemfibrozil is not in this set.

How statins injure muscle at all is still unsettled. The leading explanation is that the pathway they block also supplies coenzyme Q10 to muscle.
rules.watch: New muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness. CK. Dark or tea-colored urine means rhabdomyolysis, and creatinine next.
rules.exam: Ask about muscle symptoms at every visit, because patients write it off as having overdone it at the gym. The question that separates a complaint from an emergency is whether the urine is dark.

rules.name: Hidden acetaminophen (double dosing)
rules.mechanism:
Hydrocodone, oxycodone and codeine are usually dispensed as COMBINATION products that already contain acetaminophen. Norco, Percocet and Tylenol #3 all do.

So adding plain Tylenol on top is not a second drug. It is more of the same drug, arriving under a different name. The 4 g/day ceiling is the point where the liver starts to fail, not a suggestion, and many hospitals set their own limit at 3 g.
rules.watch: Add up acetaminophen from EVERY source: scheduled, PRN, combination opioids, and OTC cold products. Max 4 g/day, 3 g in chronic alcohol use or hepatic impairment.
rules.exam: This is the most common real-world acetaminophen overdose, and it happens to patients who were following instructions. If a question lists Percocet and Tylenol on the same MAR, that is the answer.

rules.name: Specific pairs worth knowing
rules.mechanism: Individual interactions that do not belong to a larger class.
rules.watch: Depends on the pair; each one names its own.
rules.exam: Allopurinol plus a penicillin is the sleeper here, because the consequence is a false allergy label that narrows every future antibiotic choice.

rules.name: Duplicate therapy
rules.mechanism: Two drugs doing the same job by the same mechanism. The effect doubles while the benefit does not, and on a med list it almost always means a reconciliation error rather than a plan.
rules.watch: Ask why both are on the list. This is a med-reconciliation finding more often than a prescribing one.
rules.exam: Duplicate therapy is its own category of error, separate from interaction. The ketorolac pairs are the ones with an actual labeled contraindication behind them.

rules.name: P-glycoprotein inhibition raises dabigatran
rules.mechanism:
Most drug interactions run through liver enzymes called CYP. Dabigatran does not use them at all. It depends instead on a pump in the gut wall, P-glycoprotein, that limits how much of the drug gets absorbed.

Block that pump and more dabigatran gets in, so the bleeding risk climbs. It also means dabigatran slips past every interaction warning built around liver enzymes, which is the real danger: nothing flags it.
rules.watch: Any bleeding, and renal function, since the risk concentrates at low CrCl.
rules.exam: If a question asks why dabigatran is different from apixaban and rivaroxaban pharmacokinetically, this is the answer: P-gp, not CYP3A4.

rules.name: Fluoroquinolones disturb glucose
rules.mechanism: Fluoroquinolones interfere with pancreatic beta-cell potassium channel regulation and can provoke severe hypoglycemia. The FDA required every systemic fluoroquinolone label to carry the risk of hypoglycemic coma, naming diabetic patients already on insulin or a sulfonylurea.
rules.watch: More frequent glucose checks for the duration of the antibiotic course. Risk concentrates in older adults.
rules.exam: Both directions have been reported, but hypoglycemia is the one that carries the FDA warning.

rules.name: Digoxin toxicity
rules.mechanism: Digoxin works by blocking the Na+/K+ pump. Potassium competes for that same binding site, so when potassium falls, MORE digoxin binds and a level that reads therapeutic behaves like an overdose. Low magnesium does the same thing, and high calcium adds to the contractile effect digoxin is already producing.
rules.watch: Potassium, magnesium and calcium alongside the digoxin level. Toxicity arrives in order: anorexia, then nausea and vomiting, then yellow-green visual halos, then arrhythmias.
rules.exam: Furosemide plus digoxin is the single most tested pair in cardiac pharmacology. The diuretic drops potassium, the potassium drop makes digoxin toxic, and the level never changes. Antidote is digoxin immune Fab.

rules.name: Drugs that raise the lithium level
rules.mechanism: The kidney handles lithium exactly like sodium. Anything that reduces sodium delivery or renal blood flow makes the kidney reabsorb more lithium, and the level climbs with no change in dose. Lithium has a narrow window, so a modest rise is a real toxicity.
rules.watch: Serum lithium level, sodium, hydration status. FINE tremor is expected; COARSE tremor, ataxia and slurred speech are toxicity.
rules.exam: The NSAID is the dangerous one because patients buy it over the counter without telling anyone. Any new drug in a lithium patient means rechecking the level.

rules.name: Levothyroxine absorption and effect
rules.mechanism: Levothyroxine is absorbed in a narrow window and binds readily to cations in the gut. It also accelerates the clearance of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors.
rules.watch: TSH after any change, and INR if the patient is on warfarin.
rules.exam: A patient whose TSH will not come down is usually taking levothyroxine with their calcium or iron, not failing to take it.

rules.name: Amiodarone raises other drug levels
rules.mechanism: Amiodarone inhibits CYP enzymes and P-glycoprotein, and its half-life is 40-60 days. It raises the level of several narrow-therapeutic-index drugs, and because it leaves the body so slowly, the interaction persists for WEEKS after it is stopped.
rules.watch: Digoxin level, INR, and muscle symptoms. Recheck weeks later, not days, because the interaction keeps building.
rules.exam: Amiodarone plus digoxin and amiodarone plus warfarin are both standard test items. The long half-life is the detail that makes them different from ordinary interactions.

rules.name: Stacked blood pressure lowering
rules.mechanism:
Nitroglycerin and hydralazine drop pressure fast. Added to a patient already on a beta blocker, a diuretic or a RAAS blocker, the fall can be abrupt rather than gradual.

This rule is deliberately limited to those two rapid vasodilators. Routine oral combination therapy, such as amlodipine with lisinopril, is standard practice and is NOT flagged here.
rules.watch: BP sitting and standing, heart rate, dizziness on rising, and fall risk. Hold parameters should be written for each drug.
rules.exam: Combination antihypertensive therapy is deliberate and appropriate; the nursing issue is orthostatic hypotension and falls, not that the pairing is wrong.

rules.name: Beta blockers blunt the pressors
rules.mechanism: Epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine and dobutamine all work through adrenergic receptors. A beta blocker already occupying those receptors reduces the response, so the usual dose does less than expected. With epinephrine the picture is worse: beta blockade leaves alpha effects unopposed, which can produce severe hypertension with reflex bradycardia.
rules.watch: BP and heart rate closely; expect to need higher pressor doses. Glucagon is the rescue for beta-blocker-resistant shock because it bypasses the adrenergic receptor entirely.
rules.exam: A patient on a beta blocker who has anaphylaxis may not respond to standard epinephrine dosing. That is the scenario this rule exists for.

rules.name: Anticholinergic load adds up
rules.mechanism:
Each of these blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. One drug gives you a dry mouth. Two or three give you the full picture: blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, blocked sweating so heat cannot be shed, and in older adults an acute confusion that gets charted as dementia or a UTI rather than as the drugs.

The clinical point is that total load matters, not any single drug. This is what the Beers criteria are built around, and it is the most common reversible cause of delirium in a hospitalized older adult.

The three that most often go uncounted are DIPHENHYDRAMINE (in sleep aids and cold remedies the patient does not call medication), BENZTROPINE (given to treat the side effects of an antipsychotic that is itself anticholinergic), and PROMETHAZINE. Add any two and an older adult is at real risk.
rules.watch: Mental status, which is the first thing to change in an older adult. Then bladder scan for retention, bowel sounds and last bowel movement, dry mouth and blurred vision, and temperature in hot weather.
rules.exam: The stem gives you an older adult on two or three of these who becomes confused. The answer is to look at the medication list, not to order a head CT or treat for a UTI. Count the anticholinergics.

rules.name: Stimulants push blood pressure the other way
rules.mechanism:
Methylphenidate raises synaptic norepinephrine, which raises heart rate and blood pressure. That works directly against every antihypertensive, and it adds to anything else that is already adrenergic.

Scoped to methylphenidate on purpose. DOBUTAMINE is deliberately NOT here: it is a beta-1 inotrope and its label says systemic vascular resistance is usually DECREASED, so it does not oppose an antihypertensive. Flagging it against a heart failure patient's own medication list would be backwards.
rules.watch: BP and heart rate at baseline and periodically, not just once. An antihypertensive that stopped working in a patient newly on a stimulant is the drug, not the disease.
rules.exam: The methylphenidate label says to use caution with pressor agents and to monitor BP in patients on antihypertensives. The cardiac screen before the first dose matters more than any of these pairs.

rules.name: Drugs that lower the seizure threshold
rules.mechanism:
A seizure happens when excitation outruns inhibition. Several of these drugs shift that balance a little: bupropion by raising dopamine and norepinephrine, the antipsychotics by blocking dopamine, the tricyclics through multiple receptors, methylphenidate by raising catecholamines, and the fluoroquinolones by blocking GABA-A directly.

One of them alone rarely causes a seizure in a patient with no risk factors. Stacked, or added to withdrawal, head injury, hyponatremia, an eating disorder or a prior seizure, the margin gets thin. Bupropion is the one that matters most, which is why it is in its own group.
rules.watch: Seizure history, alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, head injury, hyponatremia, eating disorder history, and renal function for the renally cleared drugs. Bupropion is dose-related, so watch for dose increases and never exceed the maximum.
rules.exam: Bupropion is the answer to 'which antidepressant is contraindicated in a patient with a seizure disorder or bulimia.' The second half of the question is usually the risk factor, not the drug: the same bupropion dose is fine in one patient and not in another.

rules.name: Ototoxicity stacks, and hearing loss is permanent
rules.mechanism:
The hair cells of the cochlea and the vestibular apparatus do not regenerate. Aminoglycosides accumulate in them and kill them. Loop diuretics damage the same structures through the ion pump in the inner ear, and high-dose IV erythromycin and vancomycin add to it.

That is the asymmetry worth holding on to: the kidney injury these drugs cause is usually reversible, and the hearing loss usually is not. So a rising creatinine is a reason to adjust, while tinnitus is a reason to stop and call.
rules.watch: Ask about tinnitus, a sense of fullness, vertigo and unsteadiness every shift, and get a baseline audiogram if therapy will run. Trough levels for gentamicin and vancomycin. Creatinine daily, since kidney and ear injury travel together.
rules.exam: The gentamicin boxed warning names potent diuretics specifically: avoid concurrent furosemide. A heart failure patient on furosemide who develops sepsis and gets gentamicin is the scenario, and the answer is to raise the combination, not to give it and watch.

rules.name: C. difficile risk, and the antidiarrheal trap
rules.mechanism:
Antibiotics kill the colonic flora that keeps Clostridioides difficile suppressed. The organism overgrows and releases toxin, which inflames the colon. It can start during therapy or up to two months after it stops.

The trap is the treatment. An ANTIMOTILITY drug such as loperamide or diphenoxylate slows the bowel and TRAPS the toxin against the mucosa, which turns colitis into ileus and toxic megacolon. Diarrhea in a patient on or recently off an antibiotic is a stool test and a phone call, never an antidiarrheal. Note that a stool SOFTENER like docusate is a different drug class and does not carry this risk. Acid suppression raises the risk further by removing the gastric barrier.
rules.watch: Stool frequency, form and character daily. New diarrhea means a stool C. difficile test, contact precautions, and SOAP AND WATER rather than alcohol gel, because the spores survive alcohol.
rules.exam: Clindamycin is the one with a boxed warning for it. The highest-yield item is the order to refuse: diarrhea on an antibiotic plus an order for loperamide means hold it, test the stool, and call.

rules.name: Never mix a penicillin and an aminoglycoside in one line
rules.mechanism:
Beta-lactams chemically INACTIVATE aminoglycosides on contact. In the patient the two are synergistic and deliberately combined, which is standard therapy in endocarditis. In the same syringe, bag or running line they destroy each other and the patient gets a fraction of the aminoglycoside dose.

So this is not a reason to avoid the combination. It is a reason to separate the administration: different times, flushed line, or a second access.

Scoped to PARENTERAL penicillins, because the interaction is physical. An oral cephalosporin or oral amoxicillin never shares a line with IV gentamicin, so there is nothing to inactivate. The documented chemistry is a penicillin-class reaction, not a cephalosporin one.
rules.watch: Administration timing and line compatibility, not a lab value. Flush between drugs, stagger the doses, and never Y-site them.
rules.exam: This is a compatibility question dressed as an interaction. The pair is therapeutically correct and the error is physical. If a stem has both hanging on one line, that is the answer.

rules.name: Alkaline solutions inactivate catecholamines
rules.mechanism:
Catecholamines are stable in acid and destroyed in base. Mixed with sodium bicarbonate, or run into a line that bicarbonate is running through, they oxidize and lose activity. The infusion keeps running, the pump keeps counting, and the patient gets nothing.

This is chemical degradation rather than a pharmacologic interaction, and it is OXIDATION rather than precipitation: the catecholamine is converted to inactive adrenochrome. That distinction matters at the bedside, because there may be no particulate to find. Checking the line for precipitate is not a valid safety check here. The only signs are a pressor requirement that climbs for no clinical reason, and sometimes a solution that has turned pink or brown. In a code, where bicarbonate and epinephrine are both being given, the answer is to flush the line between them or use a second access.
rules.watch: Not a lab value, and not a particulate check. Line separation, a flush between drugs, and a pressor requirement that suddenly climbs for no clinical reason. A solution that has turned pink or brown has already oxidized, but a clear solution is not proof that it has not.
rules.exam: Both drugs are correctly ordered and the error is physical. If a stem has bicarbonate and a pressor going through one line, that is the answer.

rules.name: Cimetidine raises other drug levels
rules.mechanism:
Cimetidine inhibits several CYP450 enzymes, so drugs cleared by them accumulate at an unchanged dose. This is not an incidental property, it is the reason famotidine replaced cimetidine in practice: famotidine does the same job at the acid pump without the interaction list.

So when a question offers both H2 blockers, cimetidine's interactions are usually why famotidine is the answer.
rules.watch: The level or effect of whatever the patient is already on: INR, phenytoin level, heart rate, sedation. Also remember cimetidine itself raises serum creatinine without changing actual renal function, which can be mistaken for kidney injury.
rules.exam: If a stem offers cimetidine and famotidine for a patient on warfarin, phenytoin or a narrow-margin drug, famotidine is the answer and the interaction list is the reason.

rules.name: Acid suppression blocks drugs that need acid
rules.mechanism:
Some drugs need an acidic stomach to dissolve or to be absorbed. Raise the pH with a proton pump inhibitor or an H2 blocker and less of the drug gets in, so the patient takes it faithfully and gets a reduced effect.

Scoped deliberately to calcium carbonate and iron, where the effect is documented and clinically visible. SUCRALFATE is NOT here: although it polymerizes in acid in vitro, its label permits antacids with only a 30-minute separation and it is routinely co-prescribed with an H2 blocker or a PPI. Sucralfate's real interaction runs the other way, binding other drugs in the gut.
rules.watch: The effect rather than a level: a calcium or iron that is not correcting, or an ulcer that is not healing on sucralfate. Calcium CITRATE does not need acid and is the better choice in a patient on a PPI.
rules.exam: A patient on omeprazole whose iron deficiency is not improving is the scenario. The answer is the absorption problem, not nonadherence and not a higher dose.

rules.name: Antithyroid drugs block radioactive iodine uptake
rules.mechanism:
Radioactive iodine is concentrated inside thyroid cells and then has to be ORGANIFIED, meaning bound into thyroid hormone, to stay there long enough to deliver its radiation. A thioamide blocks thyroid peroxidase, which is the organification step, NOT the uptake step. So the iodine still enters the cell and then washes straight back out, its effective half-life in the gland collapses, and the treatment fails.

Getting that right matters because thioamides do not reduce iodide uptake and may even increase it. A recent iodine load, including CT contrast, fails for a different reason: it floods the gland with cold iodine that competes with the radioactive dose.

Concurrent antithyroid therapy is a labeled CONTRAINDICATION to radioactive iodine, and in practice the thioamide is held for several days beforehand.
rules.watch: Whether antithyroid drugs and iodine-containing products, including recent CT contrast, have been held for the interval the protocol specifies. Afterward, free T4 and TSH as the gland is destroyed, and the transition onto levothyroxine.
rules.exam: The question is usually about preparation: what has to be stopped before the dose, and that hypothyroidism afterward is the intended result rather than a complication.

rules.name: Postpartum uterotonics work in sequence
rules.mechanism:
Oxytocin gives rhythmic contractions and is first-line for postpartum hemorrhage. Methylergonovine gives a sustained clamp and is the usual second agent when oxytocin alone has not controlled the bleeding. Using both is DELIBERATE and standard, not an error.

What makes the pair worth flagging is that their contraindications differ sharply: methylergonovine is barred by hypertension and preeclampsia, which is exactly the population most likely to be bleeding. So the second drug in the sequence may be the one you cannot give, and knowing that before the emergency is the point.
rules.watch: Blood pressure before any ergot dose, fundal tone and lochia, and for magnesium: reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output.
rules.exam: Check the blood pressure before methylergonovine is the single most tested nursing action in postpartum hemorrhage management.

rules.why: Tylenol #3 is codeine WITH acetaminophen.
Norco and Vicodin are hydrocodone WITH acetaminophen. Adding Tylenol stacks an invisible dose.
Percocet is oxycodone WITH acetaminophen. Plain oxycodone exists too, so you have to read which one was dispensed.
Sustained acetaminophen (more than ~2 g/day for several days) raises the INR. A single dose does not.

Epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine and dobutamine all work through adrenergic receptors. A beta blocker already occupying those receptors reduces the response, so the usual dose does less than expected. With epinephrine the picture is worse: beta blockade leaves alpha effects unopposed, which can produce severe hypertension with reflex bradycardia. SELECTIVITY decides this one. Propranolol and carvedilol block beta-2 as well as beta-1, so the rescue inhaler stops working and the blocker itself can cause bronchospasm. In asthma this is the classic contraindicated pairing.

Steroids drive gluconeogenesis and reduce peripheral glucose uptake, so insulin requirements rise, sometimes steeply. Beta blockers do something different and more dangerous: they mask the adrenergic warning signs of hypoglycemia (tremor, tachycardia) while sweating still comes through.

Opioids blunt the brainstem's response to rising CO₂. Benzodiazepines amplify GABA. Gabapentinoids damp excitatory transmission. Stacked, the drive to breathe can disappear while the patient simply looks asleep. The respiratory ceiling these drugs have applies only in the ABSENCE of other CNS depressants. Add a benzodiazepine and the ceiling is gone, which is the detail that makes this pair dangerous rather than reassuring.

Stopping a bleed takes two steps. Platelets clump together to form a plug, then a mesh of fibrin locks that plug in place. These drugs attack different steps.

Anticoagulants stop the fibrin mesh. Antiplatelets stop the plug. NSAIDs do two things at once by blocking COX-1: they weaken platelets AND strip the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, so you get worse clotting and a surface more likely to bleed. SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need in order to clump.

Combine any two and the risk compounds. Some of these pairs are closer to additive than multiplied, but none of them are safe to stack without watching for it.

Direct antagonism. Alteplase dissolves clot by generating plasmin; tranexamic acid blocks plasmin formation. TXA is in fact used to REVERSE alteplase bleeding, so the two together outside that rescue makes no sense.

Beta blockers slow the SA and AV node through the sympathetic pathway. Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers slow the same nodes through calcium entry. Two different doors into the same room.

Their QT effects are additive and the result is torsades, not better rhythm control. Deliberate combination is a specialist decision, not a floor one.

For the antiarrhythmics the QT effect IS the mechanism, not a side effect, which is why a class IA or class III drug can treat an arrhythmia and cause torsades with the same action. Antibiotics kill the colonic flora that keeps Clostridioides difficile suppressed. The organism overgrows and releases toxin, which inflames the colon. It can start during therapy or up to two months after it stops.

The trap is the treatment. An ANTIMOTILITY drug such as loperamide or diphenoxylate slows the bowel and TRAPS the toxin against the mucosa, which turns colitis into ileus and toxic megacolon. Diarrhea in a patient on or recently off an antibiotic is a stool test and a phone call, never an antidiarrheal. Note that a stool SOFTENER like docusate is a different drug class and does not carry this risk. Acid suppression raises the risk further by removing the gastric barrier. THE trap this rule exists for. Both labels contraindicate use in antibiotic-associated or pseudomembranous colitis. Slowing the bowel traps the toxin against the mucosa and turns colitis into ileus and toxic megacolon. Diarrhea in a patient on or recently off an antibiotic means hold the antidiarrheal, send a stool C. difficile test, and call.

Carbamazepine ↓ the DOAC level through CYP3A4 and P-gp induction → CLOT risk, with no level to warn you. The Eliquis label names carbamazepine in its AVOID sentence alongside rifampin and phenytoin.
Phenytoin ↓ the DOAC level → the patient is anticoagulated on paper and unprotected in fact → CLOT, not bleed. The Eliquis label names phenytoin in the same AVOID sentence as rifampin.

Rifampin ↓ the DOAC level through CYP3A4 and P-gp induction → CLOT risk. The Eliquis label says to AVOID combined P-gp and strong CYP3A4 inducers, naming rifampin, and there is no level to follow to tell you it has happened.

TXA preserves clot while the anticoagulant prevents it. This IS done deliberately for active bleeding in an anticoagulated patient (dental surgery, trauma), so the question is not whether to allow it but whether an indication exists. On a routine med list with no bleeding, it is a reconciliation error.
Labeled contraindication: ketorolac is contraindicated in patients currently receiving aspirin.

The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

CYCLOSPORINE belongs to the first mechanism rather than the third: its acute nephrotoxicity is AFFERENT arteriolar vasoconstriction, the same vessel an NSAID narrows, which is why cyclosporine plus an NSAID is worse than simply additive.

Gentamicin and vancomycin skip all of that and injure the tubule itself, so they add to any of the three. IV acyclovir is a third kind: it crystallizes inside the tubule when the urine is concentrated, which makes it a hydration problem rather than a dose problem, and it applies to the IV route only.

An NSAID blocks the prostaglandins, so the afferent arteriole narrows and less blood gets in. An ACE inhibitor or ARB blocks angiotensin II, so the efferent arteriole relaxes open and pressure escapes. A diuretic drops the volume arriving at both. Take all three and filtration pressure collapses. Two COX inhibitors. See the duplicate therapy and GI ulcer rules; the renal effect is additive at analgesic doses.
NSAIDs remove the prostaglandins that protect gastric mucosa. Steroids impair mucosal healing and mask the pain that would warn you. SSRIs add impaired platelet function on top.

Antihypertensives and diuretics rely partly on prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation and renal sodium handling. NSAIDs block prostaglandin synthesis, so the BP drug works less well and sodium is retained. Two COX inhibitors, which matters for bleeding and the stomach rather than for blood pressure. See those rules.

Statins, fibrates and niacin each injure muscle on their own, and together the risk climbs. Muscle pain and weakness are the warning. Rhabdomyolysis is the endpoint: muscle breaking down fast enough to damage the kidneys.

Why this is moderate and not high: the fibrate behind the serious cases is GEMFIBROZIL, which slows how fast the body clears a statin, so the statin builds up. Fenofibrate does not do that, which is exactly why it is the fibrate you pair with a statin. Gemfibrozil is not in this set.

How statins injure muscle at all is still unsettled. The leading explanation is that the pathway they block also supplies coenzyme Q10 to muscle.

Two ACE inhibitors. Pick one.

ACE inhibitors and ARBs remove aldosterone, so the kidney stops dumping K⁺. Trimethoprim blocks the distal tubule sodium channel directly, which is structurally how amiloride works. Heparin and enoxaparin suppress aldosterone synthesis in the adrenal gland, independent of their anticoagulant effect.

The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

CYCLOSPORINE belongs to the first mechanism rather than the third: its acute nephrotoxicity is AFFERENT arteriolar vasoconstriction, the same vessel an NSAID narrows, which is why cyclosporine plus an NSAID is worse than simply additive.

Gentamicin and vancomycin skip all of that and injure the tubule itself, so they add to any of the three. IV acyclovir is a third kind: it crystallizes inside the tubule when the urine is concentrated, which makes it a hydration problem rather than a dose problem, and it applies to the IV route only.

An NSAID blocks the prostaglandins, so the afferent arteriole narrows and less blood gets in. An ACE inhibitor or ARB blocks angiotensin II, so the efferent arteriole relaxes open and pressure escapes. A diuretic drops the volume arriving at both. Take all three and filtration pressure collapses.
Two ACE inhibitors. Same mechanism, no added benefit, double the hyperkalemia and kidney risk. Almost always a reconciliation error from an incomplete switch.

Same antagonism, and chlorpromazine adds marked orthostatic hypotension on top of levodopa's own.

Direct antagonism. Levodopa works by raising brain dopamine; haloperidol blocks the receptor it acts on. The antipsychotic can abolish Parkinson control within days and produce severe rigidity, and levodopa can in turn worsen psychosis. A commonly missed one: metoclopramide is a dopamine blocker given for nausea, and in a Parkinson patient it worsens rigidity and tremor and blocks the levodopa. Ondansetron does not block dopamine and is the antiemetic to use instead.
Dopamine blockade opposing levodopa. Less potent at D2 than haloperidol but still enough to worsen motor symptoms.
Same problem as metoclopramide: an antiemetic that blocks dopamine. Use ondansetron.

Promethazine is a phenothiazine and blocks dopamine, so it opposes levodopa and can worsen rigidity and tremor. Weaker than metoclopramide or prochlorperazine, but the same error, and ondansetron is the antiemetic to use in a Parkinson patient.

Beta blockers slow the SA and AV node through the sympathetic pathway. Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers slow the same nodes through calcium entry. Two different doors into the same room.

Amiodarone, digoxin and lacosamide reach the same nodes by three more routes. Most of these combinations are deliberate rate control rather than errors, so the question is almost never whether to allow the pair but what hold parameter is written and whether anyone looked at an ECG. The one pairing that genuinely stands out is a beta blocker with diltiazem or verapamil.

Antibiotics kill the colonic flora that keeps Clostridioides difficile suppressed. The organism overgrows and releases toxin, which inflames the colon. It can start during therapy or up to two months after it stops.

The trap is the treatment. An ANTIMOTILITY drug such as loperamide or diphenoxylate slows the bowel and TRAPS the toxin against the mucosa, which turns colitis into ileus and toxic megacolon. Diarrhea in a patient on or recently off an antibiotic is a stool test and a phone call, never an antidiarrheal. Note that a stool SOFTENER like docusate is a different drug class and does not carry this risk. Acid suppression raises the risk further by removing the gastric barrier. THE trap this rule exists for. Both labels contraindicate use in antibiotic-associated or pseudomembranous colitis. Slowing the bowel traps the toxin against the mucosa and turns colitis into ileus and toxic megacolon. Diarrhea in a patient on or recently off an antibiotic means hold the antidiarrheal, send a stool C. difficile test, and call.

All of these block central D2 receptors. Stack two and the blockade deepens, and so does every consequence of it: extrapyramidal symptoms, akathisia, tardive dyskinesia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

The pairing that gets missed is an antipsychotic patient who is then given metoclopramide or prochlorperazine for nausea. Ondansetron does not block dopamine and is the safer antiemetic in that patient. Two antipsychotics. A deliberate cross-taper from one agent to another is legitimate and time-limited; two standing antipsychotics with no taper plan is duplication that doubles the EPS, metabolic and NMS risk. Ask which it is.

After each beat the ventricle has to repolarize, meaning reset its electrical charge, before it can beat again. Potassium leaving the cell through the hERG channel is what does that. These drugs block hERG, so repolarization drags out. That dragged-out reset is what a long QT measures, and a beat firing during that stretched window can tip the rhythm into torsades de pointes.

They do not all carry the same weight. Ondansetron, methadone, prochlorperazine, chlorpromazine, haloperidol, amitriptyline, the fluoroquinolones and the macrolides, Bactrim, and the antiarrhythmics amiodarone and procainamide are the established ones. Loperamide belongs here only at HIGHER THAN RECOMMENDED doses, which is what its boxed warning is about. For the antiarrhythmics the QT effect IS the mechanism, not a side effect, which is why a class IA or class III drug can treat an arrhythmia and cause torsades with the same action. Escitalopram, quetiapine and olanzapine prolong QT only modestly (escitalopram by about 7 msec at 20 mg), and for metronidazole the evidence is case reports while fluoxetine's effect is marginal, so treat all of those as a reason to check rather than a reason to expect it.

The SSRI with a genuinely QT-driven dose restriction is CITALOPRAM, not escitalopram.

A seizure happens when excitation outruns inhibition. Several of these drugs shift that balance a little: bupropion by raising dopamine and norepinephrine, the antipsychotics by blocking dopamine, the tricyclics through multiple receptors, methylphenidate by raising catecholamines, and the fluoroquinolones by blocking GABA-A directly.

One of them alone rarely causes a seizure in a patient with no risk factors. Stacked, or added to withdrawal, head injury, hyponatremia, an eating disorder or a prior seizure, the margin gets thin. Bupropion is the one that matters most, which is why it is in its own group. Both shift the balance slightly. Worth noticing, and worth acting on only if the patient has another risk factor: a seizure history, withdrawal, head injury, hyponatremia or an eating disorder.

Each of these blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. One drug gives you a dry mouth. Two or three give you the full picture: blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, blocked sweating so heat cannot be shed, and in older adults an acute confusion that gets charted as dementia or a UTI rather than as the drugs.

The clinical point is that total load matters, not any single drug. This is what the Beers criteria are built around, and it is the most common reversible cause of delirium in a hospitalized older adult.

The three that most often go uncounted are DIPHENHYDRAMINE (in sleep aids and cold remedies the patient does not call medication), BENZTROPINE (given to treat the side effects of an antipsychotic that is itself anticholinergic), and PROMETHAZINE. Add any two and an older adult is at real risk.

Antibiotics kill the colonic flora that keeps Clostridioides difficile suppressed. The organism overgrows and releases toxin, which inflames the colon. It can start during therapy or up to two months after it stops.

The trap is the treatment. An ANTIMOTILITY drug such as loperamide or diphenoxylate slows the bowel and TRAPS the toxin against the mucosa, which turns colitis into ileus and toxic megacolon. Diarrhea in a patient on or recently off an antibiotic is a stool test and a phone call, never an antidiarrheal. Note that a stool SOFTENER like docusate is a different drug class and does not carry this risk. Acid suppression raises the risk further by removing the gastric barrier. THE trap this rule exists for. Both labels contraindicate use in antibiotic-associated or pseudomembranous colitis. Slowing the bowel traps the toxin against the mucosa and turns colitis into ileus and toxic megacolon. Diarrhea in a patient on or recently off an antibiotic means hold the antidiarrheal, send a stool C. difficile test, and call.

How statins injure muscle at all is still unsettled. The leading explanation is that the pathway they block also supplies coenzyme Q10 to muscle.

Two ACE inhibitors. Pick one.

ACE inhibitors and ARBs remove aldosterone, so the kidney stops dumping K⁺. Trimethoprim blocks the distal tubule sodium channel directly, which is structurally how amiloride works. Heparin and enoxaparin suppress aldosterone synthesis in the adrenal gland, independent of their anticoagulant effect.

The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

CYCLOSPORINE belongs to the first mechanism rather than the third: its acute nephrotoxicity is AFFERENT arteriolar vasoconstriction, the same vessel an NSAID narrows, which is why cyclosporine plus an NSAID is worse than simply additive.

Gentamicin and vancomycin skip all of that and injure the tubule itself, so they add to any of the three. IV acyclovir is a third kind: it crystallizes inside the tubule when the urine is concentrated, which makes it a hydration problem rather than a dose problem, and it applies to the IV route only.

An NSAID blocks the prostaglandins, so the afferent arteriole narrows and less blood gets in. An ACE inhibitor or ARB blocks angiotensin II, so the efferent arteriole relaxes open and pressure escapes. A diuretic drops the volume arriving at both. Take all three and filtration pressure collapses.

Stopping a bleed takes two steps. Platelets clump together to form a plug, then a mesh of fibrin locks that plug in place. These drugs attack different steps.

Anticoagulants stop the fibrin mesh. Antiplatelets stop the plug. NSAIDs do two things at once by blocking COX-1: they weaken platelets AND strip the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, so you get worse clotting and a surface more likely to bleed. SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need in order to clump.

Combine any two and the risk compounds. Some of these pairs are closer to additive than multiplied, but none of them are safe to stack without watching for it.

A seizure happens when excitation outruns inhibition. After each beat the ventricle has to repolarize, meaning reset its electrical charge, before it can beat again. Potassium leaving the cell through the hERG channel is what does that. These drugs block hERG, so repolarization drags out. That dragged-out reset is what a long QT measures, and a beat firing during that stretched window can tip the rhythm into torsades de pointes.

They do not all carry the same weight. The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

CYCLOSPORINE belongs to the first mechanism rather than the third: its acute nephrotoxicity is AFFERENT arteriolar vasoconstriction, the same vessel an NSAID narrows, which is why cyclosporine plus an NSAID is worse than simply additive.

Gentamicin and vancomycin skip all of that and injure the tubule itself, so they add to any of the three. IV acyclovir is a third kind: it crystallizes inside the tubule when the urine is concentrated, which makes it a hydration problem rather than a dose problem, and it applies to the IV route only.

An NSAID blocks the prostaglandins, so the afferent arteriole narrows and less blood gets in. An ACE inhibitor or ARB blocks angiotensin II, so the efferent arteriole relaxes open and pressure escapes. A diuretic drops the volume arriving at both. Take all three and filtration pressure collapses.
NSAIDs remove the prostaglandins that protect gastric mucosa. Steroids impair mucosal healing and mask the pain that would warn you. SSRIs add impaired platelet function on top.

After each beat the ventricle has to repolarize, meaning reset its electrical charge, before it can beat again. Potassium leaving the cell through the hERG channel is what does that. These drugs block hERG, so repolarization drags out. That dragged-out reset is what a long QT measures, and a beat firing during that stretched window can tip the rhythm into torsades de pointes.

They do not all carry the same weight. Ondansetron, methadone, prochlorperazine, chlorpromazine, haloperidol, amitriptyline, the fluoroquinolones and the macrolides, Bactrim, and the antiarrhythmics amiodarone and procainamide are the established ones. Loperamide belongs here only at HIGHER THAN RECOMMENDED doses, which is what its boxed warning is about. For the antiarrhythmics the QT effect IS the mechanism, not a side effect, which is why a class IA or class III drug can treat an arrhythmia and cause torsades with the same action. Escitalopram, quetiapine and olanzapine prolong QT only modestly (escitalopram by about 7 msec at 20 mg), and for metronidazole the evidence is case reports while fluoxetine's effect is marginal, so treat all of those as a reason to check rather than a reason to expect it.

The SSRI with a genuinely QT-driven dose restriction is CITALOPRAM, not escitalopram.

Each of these blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. One drug gives you a dry mouth. The clinical point is that total load matters, not any single drug. This is what the Beers criteria are built around, and it is the most common reversible cause of delirium in a hospitalized older adult.

Statins, fibrates and niacin each injure muscle on their own, and together the risk climbs. Muscle pain and weakness are the warning. Rhabdomyolysis is the endpoint: muscle breaking down fast enough to damage the kidneys.

Why this is moderate and not high: the fibrate behind the serious cases is GEMFIBROZIL, which slows how fast the body clears a statin, so the statin builds up. Fenofibrate does not do that, which is exactly why it is the fibrate you pair with a statin. Gemfibrozil is not in this set.

How statins injure muscle at all is still unsettled. The leading explanation is that the pathway they block also supplies coenzyme Q10 to muscle.

The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

CYCLOSPORINE belongs to the first mechanism rather than the third: its acute nephrotoxicity is AFFERENT arteriolar vasoconstriction, the same vessel an NSAID narrows, which is why cyclosporine plus an NSAID is worse than simply additive.

Gentamicin and vancomycin skip all of that and injure the tubule itself, so they add to any of the three. IV acyclovir is a third kind: it crystallizes inside the tubule when the urine is concentrated, which makes it a hydration problem rather than a dose problem, and it applies to the IV route only.

An NSAID blocks the prostaglandins, so the afferent arteriole narrows and less blood gets in. An ACE inhibitor or ARB blocks angiotensin II, so the efferent arteriole relaxes open and pressure escapes. A diuretic drops the volume arriving at both. Take all three and filtration pressure collapses. Both injure the tubule directly. IV acyclovir alongside gentamicin or vancomycin is a real stack: creatinine daily, hydrate, and question whether both are still needed.

Stopping a bleed takes two steps. Platelets clump together to form a plug, then a mesh of fibrin locks that plug in place. These drugs attack different steps.

Anticoagulants stop the fibrin mesh. Antiplatelets stop the plug. NSAIDs do two things at once by blocking COX-1: they weaken platelets AND strip the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, so you get worse clotting and a surface more likely to bleed. After each beat the ventricle has to repolarize, meaning reset its electrical charge, before it can beat again. Potassium leaving the cell through the hERG channel is what does that. These drugs block hERG, so repolarization drags out. That dragged-out reset is what a long QT measures, and a beat firing during that stretched window can tip the rhythm into torsades de pointes.

They do not all carry the same weight. Ondansetron, methadone, prochlorperazine, chlorpromazine, haloperidol, amitriptyline, the fluoroquinolones and the macrolides, Bactrim, and the antiarrhythmics amiodarone and procainamide are the established ones. Loperamide belongs here only at HIGHER THAN RECOMMENDED doses, which is what its boxed warning is about. For the antiarrhythmics the QT effect IS the mechanism, not a side effect, which is why a class IA or class III drug can treat an arrhythmia and cause torsades with the same action. Escitalopram, quetiapine and olanzapine prolong QT only modestly (escitalopram by about 7 msec at 20 mg), and for metronidazole the evidence is case reports while fluoxetine's effect is marginal, so treat all of those as a reason to check rather than a reason to expect it.

The SSRI with a genuinely QT-driven dose restriction is CITALOPRAM, not escitalopram.

Beta blockers slow the SA and AV node through the sympathetic pathway. Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers slow the same nodes through calcium entry. Two different doors into the same room.

Amiodarone, digoxin and lacosamide reach the same nodes by three more routes. Most of these combinations are deliberate rate control rather than errors, so the question is almost never whether to allow the pair but what hold parameter is written and whether anyone looked at an ECG. The one pairing that genuinely stands out is a beta blocker with diltiazem or verapamil. A beta blocker with amiodarone is common and guideline-supported in atrial fibrillation and after MI. The additive bradycardia and AV block are real, so hold parameters and an ECG matter, but the pairing is not an error.

Several of these drugs shift that balance a little: bupropion by raising dopamine and norepinephrine, the antipsychotics by blocking dopamine, the tricyclics through multiple receptors, methylphenidate by raising catecholamines, and the fluoroquinolones by blocking GABA-A directly.

One of them alone rarely causes a seizure in a patient with no risk factors. Stacked, or added to withdrawal, head injury, hyponatremia, an eating disorder or a prior seizure, the margin gets thin. Bupropion is the one that matters most, which is why it is in its own group.

After each beat the ventricle has to repolarize, meaning reset its electrical charge, before it can beat again. Potassium leaving the cell through the hERG channel is what does that. Two routes. All of them kill the gut bacteria that make vitamin K, which is the vitamin warfarin already works against, so the warfarin effect deepens. Metronidazole, Bactrim, erythromycin and isoniazid do something extra: they also block the enzyme that clears warfarin, so the drug itself builds up. Two hits instead of one is why those push the INR hardest.

RIFAMPIN is the exception that reverses the whole rule. It INDUCES the enzyme instead of blocking it, so the INR FALLS and the patient clots while looking anticoagulated on paper. See the induction rule.

Beta-lactams chemically INACTIVATE aminoglycosides on contact. In the patient the two are synergistic and deliberately combined, which is standard therapy in endocarditis. In the same syringe, bag or running line they destroy each other and the patient gets a fraction of the aminoglycoside dose.

So this is not a reason to avoid the combination. It is a reason to separate the administration: different times, flushed line, or a second access.

Scoped to PARENTERAL penicillins, because the interaction is physical. An oral cephalosporin or oral amoxicillin never shares a line with IV gentamicin, so there is nothing to inactivate. The documented chemistry is a penicillin-class reaction, not a cephalosporin one.

Stopping a bleed takes two steps. Platelets clump together to form a plug, then a mesh of fibrin locks that plug in place. These drugs attack different steps.

Anticoagulants stop the fibrin mesh. Antiplatelets stop the plug. NSAIDs do two things at once by blocking COX-1: they weaken platelets AND strip the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, so you get worse clotting and a surface more likely to bleed. SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need in order to clump.

Combine any two and the risk compounds. Some of these pairs are closer to additive than multiplied, but none of them are safe to stack without watching for it.

The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

CYCLOSPORINE belongs to the first mechanism rather than the third: its acute nephrotoxicity is AFFERENT arteriolar vasoconstriction, the same vessel an NSAID narrows, which is why cyclosporine plus an NSAID is worse than simply additive.

Gentamicin and vancomycin skip all of that and injure the tubule itself, so they add to any of the three. IV acyclovir is a third kind: it crystallizes inside the tubule when the urine is concentrated, which makes it a hydration problem rather than a dose problem, and it applies to the IV route only.

An NSAID blocks the prostaglandins, so the afferent arteriole narrows and less blood gets in. An ACE inhibitor or ARB blocks angiotensin II, so the efferent arteriole relaxes open and pressure escapes. A diuretic drops the volume arriving at both. Take all three and filtration pressure collapses. Two COX inhibitors. See the duplicate therapy and GI ulcer rules; the renal effect is additive at analgesic doses.
NSAIDs remove the prostaglandins that protect gastric mucosa. Steroids impair mucosal healing and mask the pain that would warn you. SSRIs add impaired platelet function on top.

Antihypertensives and diuretics rely partly on prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation and renal sodium handling. NSAIDs block prostaglandin synthesis, so the BP drug works less well and sodium is retained. Two COX inhibitors, which matters for bleeding and the stomach rather than for blood pressure. See those rules.

The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

CYCLOSPORINE belongs to the first mechanism rather than the third: its acute nephrotoxicity is AFFERENT arteriolar vasoconstriction, the same vessel an NSAID narrows, which is why cyclosporine plus an NSAID is worse than simply additive.

Gentamicin and vancomycin skip all of that and injure the tubule itself, so they add to any of the three. IV acyclovir is a third kind: it crystallizes inside the tubule when the urine is concentrated, which makes it a hydration problem rather than a dose problem, and it applies to the IV route only.

An NSAID blocks the prostaglandins, so the afferent arteriole narrows and less blood gets in. An ACE inhibitor or ARB blocks angiotensin II, so the efferent arteriole relaxes open and pressure escapes. A diuretic drops the volume arriving at both. Beta blockers slow the SA and AV node through the sympathetic pathway. Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers slow the same nodes through calcium entry. Two different doors into the same room.

Amiodarone, digoxin and lacosamide reach the same nodes by three more routes. Most of these combinations are deliberate rate control rather than errors, so the question is almost never whether to allow the pair but what hold parameter is written and whether anyone looked at an ECG. The one pairing that genuinely stands out is a beta blocker with diltiazem or verapamil. A beta blocker with digoxin is STANDARD therapy in atrial fibrillation and heart failure, not a contraindication. Both slow AV conduction, so monitor the rate and write a hold parameter.

Epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine and dobutamine all work through adrenergic receptors. A beta blocker already occupying those receptors reduces the response, so the usual dose does less than expected. With epinephrine the picture is worse: beta blockade leaves alpha effects unopposed, which can produce severe hypertension with reflex bradycardia.

Steroids drive gluconeogenesis and reduce peripheral glucose uptake, so insulin requirements rise, sometimes steeply. Beta blockers do something different and more dangerous: they mask the adrenergic warning signs of hypoglycemia (tremor, tachycardia) while sweating still comes through. Same problem as insulin and worse in one way: a sulfonylurea keeps forcing insulin out for many hours, so the hypoglycemia it causes is prolonged and recurrent, and the beta blocker has removed the tremor and tachycardia that would warn you. Treat diaphoresis as hypoglycemia until a glucose says otherwise.

Statins, fibrates and niacin each injure muscle on their own, and together the risk climbs. Muscle pain and weakness are the warning. Rhabdomyolysis is the endpoint: muscle breaking down fast enough to damage the kidneys.

Why this is moderate and not high: the fibrate behind the serious cases is GEMFIBROZIL, which slows how fast the body clears a statin, so the statin builds up. Fenofibrate does not do that, which is exactly why it is the fibrate you pair with a statin. Gemfibrozil is not in this set.

How statins injure muscle at all is still unsettled. The leading explanation is that the pathway they block also supplies coenzyme Q10 to muscle.

Low K+ and low Mg2+ lengthen the QT on their own, so they stack with a QT drug. Scoped to loop diuretics, steroids and stimulant laxatives, which drop TOTAL BODY potassium. Insulin and bicarbonate shift potassium into cells rather than removing it, and at routine dosing that shift is not a torsades risk on its own.

After each beat the ventricle has to repolarize, meaning reset its electrical charge, before it can beat again. Potassium leaving the cell through the hERG channel is what does that. These drugs block hERG, so repolarization drags out. That dragged-out reset is what a long QT measures, and a beat firing during that stretched window can tip the rhythm into torsades de pointes.

They do not all carry the same weight. Ondansetron, methadone, prochlorperazine, chlorpromazine, haloperidol, amitriptyline, the fluoroquinolones and the macrolides, Bactrim, and the antiarrhythmics amiodarone and procainamide are the established ones. Loperamide belongs here only at HIGHER THAN RECOMMENDED doses, which is what its boxed warning is about. Loperamide belongs here only at HIGHER THAN RECOMMENDED doses, which is what its boxed warning is about. For the antiarrhythmics the QT effect IS the mechanism, not a side effect, which is why a class IA or class III drug can treat an arrhythmia and cause torsades with the same action. Escitalopram, quetiapine and olanzapine prolong QT only modestly (escitalopram by about 7 msec at 20 mg), and for metronidazole the evidence is case reports while fluoxetine's effect is marginal, so treat all of those as a reason to check rather than a reason to expect it.

The SSRI with a genuinely QT-driven dose restriction is CITALOPRAM, not escitalopram.

Two routes. All of them kill the gut bacteria that make vitamin K, which is the vitamin warfarin already works against, so the warfarin effect deepens. Metronidazole, Bactrim, erythromycin and isoniazid do something extra: they also block the enzyme that clears warfarin, so the drug itself builds up. Two hits instead of one is why those push the INR hardest.

RIFAMPIN is the exception that reverses the whole rule. It INDUCES the enzyme instead of blocking it, so the INR FALLS and the patient clots while looking anticoagulated on paper. See the induction rule.

Loop diuretics dump K⁺ at the loop of Henle. Prednisone and methylprednisolone hold Na⁺ and trade away K⁺ through mineralocorticoid activity. Dexamethasone has almost none of that activity, so its hypokalemia is weaker and arrives by other routes at high dose. Insulin and sodium bicarbonate don't remove potassium at all, they drive it into cells, which looks identical on a lab draw.

Stopping a bleed takes two steps. Platelets clump together to form a plug, then a mesh of fibrin locks that plug in place. These drugs attack different steps.

Anticoagulants stop the fibrin mesh. Antiplatelets stop the plug. NSAIDs do two things at once by blocking COX-1: they weaken platelets AND strip the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, so you get worse clotting and a surface more likely to bleed. SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need in order to clump.

Combine any two and the risk compounds. Some of these pairs are closer to additive than multiplied, but none of them are safe to stack without watching for it. Bismuth subsalicylate IS a salicylate, so the hazard with warfarin or any anticoagulant is additive BLEEDING and a rising INR, not reduced absorption. Patients do not think of Pepto-Bismol as medication, let alone as aspirin, so it has to be asked about by name.

The hair cells of the cochlea and the vestibular apparatus do not regenerate. Aminoglycosides accumulate in them and kill them. Loop diuretics damage the same structures through the ion pump in the inner ear, and high-dose IV erythromycin and vancomycin add to it.

That is the asymmetry worth holding on to: the kidney injury these drugs cause is usually reversible, and the hearing loss usually is not. So a rising creatinine is a reason to adjust, while tinnitus is a reason to stop and call.

Digoxin works by blocking the Na+/K+ pump. Potassium competes for that same binding site, so when potassium falls, MORE digoxin binds and a level that reads therapeutic behaves like an overdose. Low magnesium does the same thing, and high calcium adds to the contractile effect digoxin is already producing.

A seizure happens when excitation outruns inhibition. Several of these drugs shift that balance a little: bupropion by raising dopamine and norepinephrine, the antipsychotics by blocking dopamine, the tricyclics through multiple receptors, methylphenidate by raising catecholamines, and the fluoroquinolones by blocking GABA-A directly.

One of them alone rarely causes a seizure in a patient with no risk factors. Stacked, or added to withdrawal, head injury, hyponatremia, an eating disorder or a prior seizure, the margin gets thin. Bupropion is the one that matters most, which is why it is in its own group.

The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

CYCLOSPORINE belongs to the first mechanism rather than the third: its acute nephrotoxicity is AFFERENT arteriolar vasoconstriction, the same vessel an NSAID narrows, which is why cyclosporine plus an NSAID is worse than simply additive.

Gentamicin and vancomycin skip all of that and injure the tubule itself, so they add to any of the three. IV acyclovir is a third kind: it crystallizes inside the tubule when the urine is concentrated, which makes it a hydration problem rather than a dose problem, and it applies to the IV route only.

An NSAID blocks the prostaglandins, so the afferent arteriole narrows and less blood gets in. An ACE inhibitor or ARB blocks angiotensin II, so the efferent arteriole relaxes open and pressure escapes. A diuretic drops the volume arriving at both. Take all three and filtration pressure collapses.

Antihypertensives and diuretics rely partly on prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation and renal sodium handling. NSAIDs block prostaglandin synthesis, so the BP drug works less well and sodium is retained.

ACE inhibitors and ARBs remove aldosterone, so the kidney stops dumping K⁺. Trimethoprim blocks the distal tubule sodium channel directly, which is structurally how amiloride works. Heparin and enoxaparin suppress aldosterone synthesis in the adrenal gland, independent of their anticoagulant effect.

Beta blockers slow the SA and AV node through the sympathetic pathway. Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers slow the same nodes through calcium entry. Two different doors into the same room.

Amiodarone, digoxin and lacosamide reach the same nodes by three more routes. Most of these combinations are deliberate rate control rather than errors, so the question is almost never whether to allow the pair but what hold parameter is written and whether anyone looked at an ECG. The one pairing that genuinely stands out is a beta blocker with diltiazem or verapamil. A beta blocker with digoxin is STANDARD therapy in atrial fibrillation and heart failure, not a contraindication. Both slow AV conduction, so monitor the rate and write a hold parameter.

Each of these blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. One drug gives you a dry mouth. Two or three give you the full picture: blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, blocked sweating so heat cannot be shed, and in older adults an acute confusion that gets charted as dementia or a UTI rather than as the drugs.

The clinical point is that total load matters, not any single drug. This is what the Beers criteria are built around, and it is the most common reversible cause of delirium in a hospitalized older adult.

The three that most often go uncounted are DIPHENHYDRAMINE (in sleep aids and cold remedies the patient does not call medication), BENZTROPINE (given to treat the side effects of an antipsychotic that is itself anticholinergic), and PROMETHAZINE. Add any two and an older adult is at real risk.
