Antibiotics kill the colonic flora that keeps Clostridioides difficile suppressed. The organism overgrows and releases toxin, which inflames the colon. It can start during therapy or up to two months after it stops.

The trap is the treatment. An ANTIMOTILITY drug such as loperamide or diphenoxylate slows the bowel and TRAPS the toxin against the mucosa, which turns colitis into ileus and toxic megacolon. Diarrhea in a patient on or recently off an antibiotic is a stool test and a phone call, never an antidiarrheal. Note that a stool SOFTENER like docusate is a different drug class and does not carry this risk. Acid suppression raises the risk further by removing the gastric barrier.

Two routes. All of them kill the gut bacteria that make vitamin K, which is the vitamin warfarin already works against, so the warfarin effect deepens. Metronidazole, Bactrim, erythromycin and isoniazid do something extra: they also block the enzyme that clears warfarin, so the drug itself builds up. Two hits instead of one is why those push the INR hardest.

RIFAMPIN is the exception that reverses the whole rule. It INDUCES the enzyme instead of blocking it, so the INR FALLS and the patient clots while looking anticoagulated on paper. See the induction rule.

Stopping a bleed takes two steps. Platelets clump together to form a plug, then a mesh of fibrin locks that plug in place. These drugs attack different steps.

Anticoagulants stop the fibrin mesh. Antiplatelets stop the plug. NSAIDs do two things at once by blocking COX-1: they weaken platelets AND strip the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, so you get worse clotting and a surface more likely to bleed. SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need in order to clump.

Combine any two and the risk compounds. Some of these pairs are closer to additive than multiplied, but none of them are safe to stack without watching for it.

Opioids blunt the brainstem's response to rising CO₂. Benzodiazepines amplify GABA. Gabapentinoids damp excitatory transmission. Stacked, the drive to breathe can disappear while the patient simply looks asleep. Additive sedation, plus additive constipation and urinary retention. Promethazine with an opioid is a very common pairing for nausea, so expect it and monitor rather than treating it as an error.

Stacked, the drive to breathe can disappear while the patient simply looks asleep. A long-acting opioid plus a short-acting one for breakthrough is STANDARD practice. Two scheduled long-acting opioids is duplication. Judge by the roles.

The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

CYCLOSPORINE belongs to the first mechanism rather than the third: its acute nephrotoxicity is AFFERENT arteriolar vasoconstriction, the same vessel an NSAID narrows, which is why cyclosporine plus an NSAID is worse than simply additive.

Gentamicin and vancomycin skip all of that and injure the tubule itself, so they add to any of the three. IV acyclovir is a third kind: it crystallizes inside the tubule when the urine is concentrated, which makes it a hydration problem rather than a dose problem, and it applies to the IV route only.

An NSAID blocks the prostaglandins, so the afferent arteriole narrows and less blood gets in. An ACE inhibitor or ARB blocks angiotensin II, so the efferent arteriole relaxes open and pressure escapes. A diuretic drops the volume arriving at both. Take all three and filtration pressure collapses.

Several of these drugs shift that balance a little: bupropion by raising dopamine and norepinephrine, the antipsychotics by blocking dopamine, the tricyclics through multiple receptors, methylphenidate by raising catecholamines, and the fluoroquinolones by blocking GABA-A directly.

One of them alone rarely causes a seizure in a patient with no risk factors. Stacked, or added to withdrawal, head injury, hyponatremia, an eating disorder or a prior seizure, the margin gets thin. Bupropion is the one that matters most, which is why it is in its own group. Weak. Flagged through the fluoroquinolone link rather than on its own.

Statins, fibrates and niacin each injure muscle on their own, and together the risk climbs. Muscle pain and weakness are the warning. Rhabdomyolysis is the endpoint: muscle breaking down fast enough to damage the kidneys.

Why this is moderate and not high: the fibrate behind the serious cases is GEMFIBROZIL, which slows how fast the body clears a statin, so the statin builds up. Fenofibrate does not do that, which is exactly why it is the fibrate you pair with a statin. Gemfibrozil is not in this set.

How statins injure muscle at all is still unsettled. The leading explanation is that the pathway they block also supplies coenzyme Q10 to muscle.

ACE inhibitors and ARBs remove aldosterone, so the kidney stops dumping K⁺. Trimethoprim blocks the distal tubule sodium channel directly, which is structurally how amiloride works. Heparin and enoxaparin suppress aldosterone synthesis in the adrenal gland, independent of their anticoagulant effect.

The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

CYCLOSPORINE belongs to the first mechanism rather than the third: its acute nephrotoxicity is AFFERENT arteriolar vasoconstriction, the same vessel an NSAID narrows, which is why cyclosporine plus an NSAID is worse than simply additive.

Gentamicin and vancomycin skip all of that and injure the tubule itself, so they add to any of the three. IV acyclovir is a third kind: it crystallizes inside the tubule when the urine is concentrated, which makes it a hydration problem rather than a dose problem, and it applies to the IV route only.

Stopping a bleed takes two steps. Platelets clump together to form a plug, then a mesh of fibrin locks that plug in place. These drugs attack different steps.

Anticoagulants stop the fibrin mesh. Antiplatelets stop the plug. NSAIDs do two things at once by blocking COX-1: they weaken platelets AND strip the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, so you get worse clotting and a surface more likely to bleed. SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need in order to clump.

Combine any two and the risk compounds. Some of these pairs are closer to additive than multiplied, but none of them are safe to stack without watching for it.

Digoxin works by blocking the Na+/K+ pump. Potassium competes for that same binding site, so when potassium falls, MORE digoxin binds and a level that reads therapeutic behaves like an overdose. Low magnesium does the same thing, and high calcium adds to the contractile effect digoxin is already producing.
NSAIDs remove the prostaglandins that protect gastric mucosa. Steroids impair mucosal healing and mask the pain that would warn you. SSRIs add impaired platelet function on top.

Insulin and bicarbonate shift potassium into cells rather than removing it, and at routine dosing that shift is not a torsades risk on its own.

Dexamethasone has almost none of that activity, so its hypokalemia is weaker and arrives by other routes at high dose. Insulin and sodium bicarbonate don't remove potassium at all, they drive it into cells, which looks identical on a lab draw.

Beta blockers slow the SA and AV node through the sympathetic pathway. Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers slow the same nodes through calcium entry. Two different doors into the same room.

Amiodarone, digoxin and lacosamide reach the same nodes by three more routes. Most of these combinations are deliberate rate control rather than errors, so the question is almost never whether to allow the pair but what hold parameter is written and whether anyone looked at an ECG. The one pairing that genuinely stands out is a beta blocker with diltiazem or verapamil. Two problems at once: additive AV block, and verapamil in particular RAISES the digoxin level. Check a digoxin level, not just the heart rate.

Erythromycin roughly DOUBLES digoxin exposure, by two routes at once: it inhibits the P-glycoprotein that pumps digoxin out, and it kills the colonic bacteria that inactivate a share of each oral dose. Check a digoxin level and watch for nausea, visual halos and bradycardia.

A seizure happens when excitation outruns inhibition. Several of these drugs shift that balance a little: bupropion by raising dopamine and norepinephrine, the antipsychotics by blocking dopamine, the tricyclics through multiple receptors, methylphenidate by raising catecholamines, and the fluoroquinolones by blocking GABA-A directly.

One of them alone rarely causes a seizure in a patient with no risk factors. Stacked, or added to withdrawal, head injury, hyponatremia, an eating disorder or a prior seizure, the margin gets thin. Bupropion is the one that matters most, which is why it is in its own group. Both shift the balance slightly. Worth noticing, and worth acting on only if the patient has another risk factor: a seizure history, withdrawal, head injury, hyponatremia or an eating disorder.

Antibiotics kill the colonic flora that keeps Clostridioides difficile suppressed. The organism overgrows and releases toxin, which inflames the colon. It can start during therapy or up to two months after it stops.

The trap is the treatment. An ANTIMOTILITY drug such as loperamide or diphenoxylate slows the bowel and TRAPS the toxin against the mucosa, which turns colitis into ileus and toxic megacolon. Diarrhea in a patient on or recently off an antibiotic is a stool test and a phone call, never an antidiarrheal. Note that a stool SOFTENER like docusate is a different drug class and does not carry this risk. Acid suppression raises the risk further by removing the gastric barrier.

Epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine and dobutamine all work through adrenergic receptors. A beta blocker already occupying those receptors reduces the response, so the usual dose does less than expected. With epinephrine the picture is worse: beta blockade leaves alpha effects unopposed, which can produce severe hypertension with reflex bradycardia.

Catecholamines are stable in acid and destroyed in base. Mixed with sodium bicarbonate, or run into a line that bicarbonate is running through, they oxidize and lose activity. The infusion keeps running, the pump keeps counting, and the patient gets nothing.

This is chemical degradation rather than a pharmacologic interaction, and it is OXIDATION rather than precipitation: the catecholamine is converted to inactive adrenochrome. That distinction matters at the bedside, because there may be no particulate to find. Checking the line for precipitate is not a valid safety check here. The only signs are a pressor requirement that climbs for no clinical reason, and sometimes a solution that has turned pink or brown. In a code, where bicarbonate and epinephrine are both being given, the answer is to flush the line between them or use a second access.

Furosemide injection has a pH of 8.0 to 9.3 and is documented incompatible with dopamine. Note this is dopamine-specific: epinephrine and norepinephrine are listed as Y-site compatible with furosemide, so do not generalize it to the whole group.
Additive catecholamine effect, and dopamine at pressor doses raises blood pressure through the same alpha receptors.

Catecholamines are stable in acid and destroyed in base. Mixed with sodium bicarbonate, or run into a line that bicarbonate is running through, they oxidize and lose activity. The infusion keeps running, the pump keeps counting, and the patient gets nothing.

This is chemical degradation rather than a pharmacologic interaction, and it is OXIDATION rather than precipitation: the catecholamine is converted to inactive adrenochrome. That distinction matters at the bedside, because there may be no particulate to find. Checking the line for precipitate is not a valid safety check here. The only signs are a pressor requirement that climbs for no clinical reason, and sometimes a solution that has turned pink or brown. In a code, where bicarbonate and epinephrine are both being given, the answer is to flush the line between them or use a second access.

Two routes. All of them kill the gut bacteria that make vitamin K, which is the vitamin warfarin already works against, so the warfarin effect deepens. Stopping a bleed takes two steps. Platelets clump together to form a plug, then a mesh of fibrin locks that plug in place. These drugs attack different steps.

Anticoagulants stop the fibrin mesh. Antiplatelets stop the plug. NSAIDs do two things at once by blocking COX-1: they weaken platelets AND strip the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, so you get worse clotting and a surface more likely to bleed. SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need in order to clump.

Combine any two and the risk compounds. Some of these pairs are closer to additive than multiplied, but none of them are safe to stack without watching for it.

ACE inhibitors and ARBs remove aldosterone, so the kidney stops dumping K⁺. Trimethoprim blocks the distal tubule sodium channel directly, which is structurally how amiloride works. Heparin and enoxaparin suppress aldosterone synthesis in the adrenal gland, independent of their anticoagulant effect.

The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

CYCLOSPORINE belongs to the first mechanism rather than the third: its acute nephrotoxicity is AFFERENT arteriolar vasoconstriction, the same vessel an NSAID narrows, which is why cyclosporine plus an NSAID is worse than simply additive.

Gentamicin and vancomycin skip all of that and injure the tubule itself, so they add to any of the three. IV acyclovir is a third kind: it crystallizes inside the tubule when the urine is concentrated, which makes it a hydration problem rather than a dose problem, and it applies to the IV route only.

An NSAID blocks the prostaglandins, so the afferent arteriole narrows and less blood gets in. An ACE inhibitor or ARB blocks angiotensin II, so the efferent arteriole relaxes open and pressure escapes. A diuretic drops the volume arriving at both. Take all three and filtration pressure collapses.

Stopping a bleed takes two steps. Platelets clump together to form a plug, then a mesh of fibrin locks that plug in place. These drugs attack different steps.

Catecholamines are stable in acid and destroyed in base. Mixed with sodium bicarbonate, or run into a line that bicarbonate is running through, they oxidize and lose activity. The infusion keeps running, the pump keeps counting, and the patient gets nothing.

This is chemical degradation rather than a pharmacologic interaction, and it is OXIDATION rather than precipitation: the catecholamine is converted to inactive adrenochrome. That distinction matters at the bedside, because there may be no particulate to find. Checking the line for precipitate is not a valid safety check here. The only signs are a pressor requirement that climbs for no clinical reason, and sometimes a solution that has turned pink or brown. In a code, where bicarbonate and epinephrine are both being given, the answer is to flush the line between them or use a second access.

After each beat the ventricle has to repolarize, meaning reset its electrical charge, before it can beat again. Potassium leaving the cell through the hERG channel is what does that. The hair cells of the cochlea and the vestibular apparatus do not regenerate. Aminoglycosides accumulate in them and kill them. Loop diuretics damage the same structures through the ion pump in the inner ear, and high-dose IV erythromycin and vancomycin add to it.

That is the asymmetry worth holding on to: the kidney injury these drugs cause is usually reversible, and the hearing loss usually is not. So a rising creatinine is a reason to adjust, while tinnitus is a reason to stop and call. Weaker on both sides. Anticoagulants stop the fibrin mesh. Antiplatelets stop the plug. Antibiotics kill the colonic flora that keeps Clostridioides difficile suppressed. The organism overgrows and releases toxin, which inflames the colon. It can start during therapy or up to two months after it stops.

The trap is the treatment. An ANTIMOTILITY drug such as loperamide or diphenoxylate slows the bowel and TRAPS the toxin against the mucosa, which turns colitis into ileus and toxic megacolon. Diarrhea in a patient on or recently off an antibiotic is a stool test and a phone call, never an antidiarrheal. Note that a stool SOFTENER like docusate is a different drug class and does not carry this risk. Acid suppression raises the risk further by removing the gastric barrier.

Opioids blunt the brainstem's response to rising CO₂. Benzodiazepines amplify GABA. Gabapentinoids damp excitatory transmission. Stacked, the drive to breathe can disappear while the patient simply looks asleep. A long-acting opioid plus a short-acting one for breakthrough is STANDARD practice. Two scheduled long-acting opioids is duplication. Judge by the roles.

Stopping a bleed takes two steps. Platelets clump together to form a plug, then a mesh of fibrin locks that plug in place. These drugs attack different steps.

Anticoagulants stop the fibrin mesh. Antiplatelets stop the plug. NSAIDs do two things at once by blocking COX-1: they weaken platelets AND strip the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, so you get worse clotting and a surface more likely to bleed. SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need in order to clump.

Combine any two and the risk compounds. Some of these pairs are closer to additive than multiplied, but none of them are safe to stack without watching for it.

The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

CYCLOSPORINE belongs to the first mechanism rather than the third: its acute nephrotoxicity is AFFERENT arteriolar vasoconstriction, the same vessel an NSAID narrows, which is why cyclosporine plus an NSAID is worse than simply additive.

Gentamicin and vancomycin skip all of that and injure the tubule itself, so they add to any of the three. Watch respiratory rate and sedation, especially in older adults, in renal impairment and in COPD.

Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

CYCLOSPORINE belongs to the first mechanism rather than the third: its acute nephrotoxicity is AFFERENT arteriolar vasoconstriction, the same vessel an NSAID narrows, which is why cyclosporine plus an NSAID is worse than simply additive.

Gentamicin and vancomycin skip all of that and injure the tubule itself, so they add to any of the three. IV acyclovir is a third kind: it crystallizes inside the tubule when the urine is concentrated, which makes it a hydration problem rather than a dose problem, and it applies to the IV route only.

Stopping a bleed takes two steps. Platelets clump together to form a plug, then a mesh of fibrin locks that plug in place. These drugs attack different steps.

Anticoagulants stop the fibrin mesh. Antiplatelets stop the plug. NSAIDs do two things at once by blocking COX-1: they weaken platelets AND strip the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, so you get worse clotting and a surface more likely to bleed. SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need in order to clump.

Combine any two and the risk compounds. Some of these pairs are closer to additive than multiplied, but none of them are safe to stack without watching for it.

Stopping a bleed takes two steps. Platelets clump together to form a plug, then a mesh of fibrin locks that plug in place. These drugs attack different steps.

Anticoagulants stop the fibrin mesh. Antiplatelets stop the plug. NSAIDs do two things at once by blocking COX-1: they weaken platelets AND strip the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, so you get worse clotting and a surface more likely to bleed. SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need in order to clump.

Combine any two and the risk compounds. Some of these pairs are closer to additive than multiplied, but none of them are safe to stack without watching for it.

Steroids drive gluconeogenesis and reduce peripheral glucose uptake, so insulin requirements rise, sometimes steeply. Beta blockers do something different and more dangerous: they mask the adrenergic warning signs of hypoglycemia (tremor, tachycardia) while sweating still comes through.

Loop diuretics dump K⁺ at the loop of Henle. Prednisone and methylprednisolone hold Na⁺ and trade away K⁺ through mineralocorticoid activity. Dexamethasone has almost none of that activity, so its hypokalemia is weaker and arrives by other routes at high dose. Insulin and sodium bicarbonate don't remove potassium at all, they drive it into cells, which looks identical on a lab draw.

The opposite direction from the rest of this rule: isoniazid INHIBITS the enzyme that clears phenytoin, so the phenytoin level CLIMBS into the toxic range on an unchanged dose. Watch for ataxia, nystagmus and slurred speech, and check a level.

Standard TB therapy, given together on purpose. The issue is not the pairing but that their HEPATOTOXICITY is additive: monitor AST, ALT and bilirubin, and treat new nausea, anorexia or jaundice as a drug problem until proven otherwise. One more trap: if this patient is also on PHENYTOIN, the two TB drugs push its level in OPPOSITE directions, isoniazid up and rifampin down, so the level is unpredictable rather than simply low. Measure it; do not reason it out.

Two routes. All of them kill the gut bacteria that make vitamin K, which is the vitamin warfarin already works against, so the warfarin effect deepens. Metronidazole, Bactrim, erythromycin and isoniazid do something extra: they also block the enzyme that clears warfarin, so the drug itself builds up. Two hits instead of one is why those push the INR hardest.

RIFAMPIN is the exception that reverses the whole rule. It INDUCES the enzyme instead of blocking it, so the INR FALLS and the patient clots while looking anticoagulated on paper. See the induction rule.

The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

CYCLOSPORINE belongs to the first mechanism rather than the third: its acute nephrotoxicity is AFFERENT arteriolar vasoconstriction, the same vessel an NSAID narrows, which is why cyclosporine plus an NSAID is worse than simply additive.

Gentamicin and vancomycin skip all of that and injure the tubule itself, so they add to any of the three. IV acyclovir is a third kind: it crystallizes inside the tubule when the urine is concentrated, which makes it a hydration problem rather than a dose problem, and it applies to the IV route only.

An NSAID blocks the prostaglandins, so the afferent arteriole narrows and less blood gets in. An ACE inhibitor or ARB blocks angiotensin II, so the efferent arteriole relaxes open and pressure escapes. A diuretic drops the volume arriving at both. Take all three and filtration pressure collapses.

Antihypertensives and diuretics rely partly on prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation and renal sodium handling. NSAIDs block prostaglandin synthesis, so the BP drug works less well and sodium is retained.

The kidney handles lithium exactly like sodium. Anything that reduces sodium delivery or renal blood flow makes the kidney reabsorb more lithium, and the level climbs with no change in dose. Lithium has a narrow window, so a modest rise is a real toxicity.

Stopping a bleed takes two steps. Platelets clump together to form a plug, then a mesh of fibrin locks that plug in place. These drugs attack different steps.

Anticoagulants stop the fibrin mesh. Antiplatelets stop the plug. NSAIDs do two things at once by blocking COX-1: they weaken platelets AND strip the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, so you get worse clotting and a surface more likely to bleed. SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need in order to clump.

Combine any two and the risk compounds. Some of these pairs are closer to additive than multiplied, but none of them are safe to stack without watching for it.

Beta blockers slow the SA and AV node through the sympathetic pathway. Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers slow the same nodes through calcium entry. Two different doors into the same room.

Amiodarone, digoxin and lacosamide reach the same nodes by three more routes. Most of these combinations are deliberate rate control rather than errors, so the question is almost never whether to allow the pair but what hold parameter is written and whether anyone looked at an ECG. The one pairing that genuinely stands out is a beta blocker with diltiazem or verapamil. Additive PR prolongation. Get a baseline ECG rather than avoiding the pair.

Opioids blunt the brainstem's response to rising CO₂. Benzodiazepines amplify GABA. Gabapentinoids damp excitatory transmission. Stacked, the drive to breathe can disappear while the patient simply looks asleep. In status epilepticus this is the GUIDELINE sequence, not a conflict: a benzodiazepine first to stop the seizure, then levetiracetam to keep it stopped. Additive sedation is expected. Watch the airway and respiratory rate, which is what you would be doing anyway.

After each beat the ventricle has to repolarize, meaning reset its electrical charge, before it can beat again. Potassium leaving the cell through the hERG channel is what does that. These drugs block hERG, so repolarization drags out. That dragged-out reset is what a long QT measures, and a beat firing during that stretched window can tip the rhythm into torsades de pointes.

They do not all carry the same weight. Ondansetron, methadone, prochlorperazine, chlorpromazine, haloperidol, amitriptyline, the fluoroquinolones and the macrolides, Bactrim, and the antiarrhythmics amiodarone and procainamide are the established ones. Loperamide belongs here only at HIGHER THAN RECOMMENDED doses, which is what its boxed warning is about. Loperamide belongs here only at HIGHER THAN RECOMMENDED doses, which is what its boxed warning is about. For the antiarrhythmics the QT effect IS the mechanism, not a side effect, which is why a class IA or class III drug can treat an arrhythmia and cause torsades with the same action. Escitalopram, quetiapine and olanzapine prolong QT only modestly (escitalopram by about 7 msec at 20 mg), and for metronidazole the evidence is case reports while fluoxetine's effect is marginal, so treat all of those as a reason to check rather than a reason to expect it.

The SSRI with a genuinely QT-driven dose restriction is CITALOPRAM, not escitalopram.

Low K+ and low Mg2+ lengthen the QT on their own, so they stack with a QT drug. Scoped to loop diuretics, steroids and stimulant laxatives, which drop TOTAL BODY potassium. Insulin and bicarbonate shift potassium into cells rather than removing it, and at routine dosing that shift is not a torsades risk on its own.
Same labeled warning: corticosteroids further raise fluoroquinolone tendon rupture risk.

A seizure happens when excitation outruns inhibition. Several of these drugs shift that balance a little: bupropion by raising dopamine and norepinephrine, the antipsychotics by blocking dopamine, the tricyclics through multiple receptors, methylphenidate by raising catecholamines, and the fluoroquinolones by blocking GABA-A directly.

One of them alone rarely causes a seizure in a patient with no risk factors. Stacked, or added to withdrawal, head injury, hyponatremia, an eating disorder or a prior seizure, the margin gets thin. Bupropion is the one that matters most, which is why it is in its own group. Overlapping membership; the fluoroquinolone is already counted in the contributes group.

A seizure happens when excitation outruns inhibition. Several of these drugs shift that balance a little: bupropion by raising dopamine and norepinephrine, the antipsychotics by blocking dopamine, the tricyclics through multiple receptors, methylphenidate by raising catecholamines, and the fluoroquinolones by blocking GABA-A directly.

One of them alone rarely causes a seizure in a patient with no risk factors. Stacked, or added to withdrawal, head injury, hyponatremia, an eating disorder or a prior seizure, the margin gets thin. Bupropion is the one that matters most, which is why it is in its own group. Overlapping membership; the fluoroquinolone is already counted in the contributes group.

Two routes. All of them kill the gut bacteria that make vitamin K, which is the vitamin warfarin already works against, so the warfarin effect deepens. Metronidazole, Bactrim, erythromycin and isoniazid do something extra: they also block the enzyme that clears warfarin, so the drug itself builds up. Two hits instead of one is why those push the INR hardest.

RIFAMPIN is the exception that reverses the whole rule. It INDUCES the enzyme instead of blocking it, so the INR FALLS and the patient clots while looking anticoagulated on paper. See the induction rule.

The kidney handles lithium exactly like sodium. Anything that reduces sodium delivery or renal blood flow makes the kidney reabsorb more lithium, and the level climbs with no change in dose. Lithium has a narrow window, so a modest rise is a real toxicity.

The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

CYCLOSPORINE belongs to the first mechanism rather than the third: its acute nephrotoxicity is AFFERENT arteriolar vasoconstriction, the same vessel an NSAID narrows, which is why cyclosporine plus an NSAID is worse than simply additive.

Gentamicin and vancomycin skip all of that and injure the tubule itself, so they add to any of the three. IV acyclovir is a third kind: it crystallizes inside the tubule when the urine is concentrated, which makes it a hydration problem rather than a dose problem, and it applies to the IV route only.

An NSAID blocks the prostaglandins, so the afferent arteriole narrows and less blood gets in. An ACE inhibitor or ARB blocks angiotensin II, so the efferent arteriole relaxes open and pressure escapes. A diuretic drops the volume arriving at both. Take all three and filtration pressure collapses.

Antihypertensives and diuretics rely partly on prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation and renal sodium handling. NSAIDs block prostaglandin synthesis, so the BP drug works less well and sodium is retained.

ACE inhibitors and ARBs remove aldosterone, so the kidney stops dumping K⁺. Trimethoprim blocks the distal tubule sodium channel directly, which is structurally how amiloride works. Heparin and enoxaparin suppress aldosterone synthesis in the adrenal gland, independent of their anticoagulant effect.

Too much serotonin at the synapse. The SSRIs and SNRIs here (fluoxetine, sertraline, escitalopram, venlafaxine, duloxetine) raise it directly by blocking its reuptake. Amitriptyline does the same, alongside norepinephrine. Methadone and buspirone contribute weakly.

Ondansetron and metoclopramide are a different case. They BLOCK serotonin receptors rather than raising serotonin, and the link to serotonin syndrome rests on case reports with no established mechanism. Treat them as a reason to look, not a reason to expect it. Lithium augmentation of an SSRI or SNRI is DELIBERATE, guideline-supported therapy for treatment-resistant depression, so this is not an error. But serotonin toxicity is described with the combination, and the picture overlaps with lithium toxicity itself (tremor, confusion, GI upset), so the two get confused. Check a lithium level before assuming serotonin syndrome.

Antibiotics kill the colonic flora that keeps Clostridioides difficile suppressed. The organism overgrows and releases toxin, which inflames the colon. It can start during therapy or up to two months after it stops.

The trap is the treatment. An ANTIMOTILITY drug such as loperamide or diphenoxylate slows the bowel and TRAPS the toxin against the mucosa, which turns colitis into ileus and toxic megacolon. Diarrhea in a patient on or recently off an antibiotic is a stool test and a phone call, never an antidiarrheal. Note that a stool SOFTENER like docusate is a different drug class and does not carry this risk. Acid suppression raises the risk further by removing the gastric barrier.

The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

CYCLOSPORINE belongs to the first mechanism rather than the third: its acute nephrotoxicity is AFFERENT arteriolar vasoconstriction, the same vessel an NSAID narrows, which is why cyclosporine plus an NSAID is worse than simply additive.

Gentamicin and vancomycin skip all of that and injure the tubule itself, so they add to any of the three. IV acyclovir is a third kind: it crystallizes inside the tubule when the urine is concentrated, which makes it a hydration problem rather than a dose problem, and it applies to the IV route only.

An NSAID blocks the prostaglandins, so the afferent arteriole narrows and less blood gets in. An ACE inhibitor or ARB blocks angiotensin II, so the efferent arteriole relaxes open and pressure escapes. A diuretic drops the volume arriving at both. Take all three and filtration pressure collapses.

Antihypertensives and diuretics rely partly on prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation and renal sodium handling. NSAIDs block prostaglandin synthesis, so the BP drug works less well and sodium is retained.

ACE inhibitors and ARBs remove aldosterone, so the kidney stops dumping K⁺. Trimethoprim blocks the distal tubule sodium channel directly, which is structurally how amiloride works. Heparin and enoxaparin suppress aldosterone synthesis in the adrenal gland, independent of their anticoagulant effect.

Too much serotonin at the synapse. The SSRIs and SNRIs here (fluoxetine, sertraline, escitalopram, venlafaxine, duloxetine) raise it directly by blocking its reuptake. Amitriptyline does the same, alongside norepinephrine. Methadone and buspirone contribute weakly.

Ondansetron and metoclopramide are a different case. They BLOCK serotonin receptors rather than raising serotonin, and the link to serotonin syndrome rests on case reports with no established mechanism. Treat them as a reason to look, not a reason to expect it. Two weak contributors. Ondansetron with metoclopramide is routine combination antiemetic therapy, and both of them BLOCK serotonin receptors rather than raising synaptic serotonin, so calling this a serotonin syndrome pair overstates the mechanism. A reason to look if the patient is also on something serotonergic, nothing more.

A seizure happens when excitation outruns inhibition. Several of these drugs shift that balance a little: bupropion by raising dopamine and norepinephrine, the antipsychotics by blocking dopamine, the tricyclics through multiple receptors, methylphenidate by raising catecholamines, and the fluoroquinolones by blocking GABA-A directly.

One of them alone rarely causes a seizure in a patient with no risk factors. Stacked, or added to withdrawal, head injury, hyponatremia, an eating disorder or a prior seizure, the margin gets thin. Bupropion is the one that matters most, which is why it is in its own group. Both shift the balance slightly. Worth noticing, and worth acting on only if the patient has another risk factor: a seizure history, withdrawal, head injury, hyponatremia or an eating disorder.

Low K+ and low Mg2+ lengthen the QT on their own, so they stack with a QT drug. Scoped to loop diuretics, steroids and stimulant laxatives, which drop TOTAL BODY potassium. Insulin and bicarbonate shift potassium into cells rather than removing it, and at routine dosing that shift is not a torsades risk on its own.

After each beat the ventricle has to repolarize, meaning reset its electrical charge, before it can beat again. Potassium leaving the cell through the hERG channel is what does that. These drugs block hERG, so repolarization drags out. That dragged-out reset is what a long QT measures, and a beat firing during that stretched window can tip the rhythm into torsades de pointes.

They do not all carry the same weight. Ondansetron, methadone, prochlorperazine, chlorpromazine, haloperidol, amitriptyline, the fluoroquinolones and the macrolides, Bactrim, and the antiarrhythmics amiodarone and procainamide are the established ones. Loperamide belongs here only at HIGHER THAN RECOMMENDED doses, which is what its boxed warning is about. Loperamide belongs here only at HIGHER THAN RECOMMENDED doses, which is what its boxed warning is about. For the antiarrhythmics the QT effect IS the mechanism, not a side effect, which is why a class IA or class III drug can treat an arrhythmia and cause torsades with the same action. Escitalopram, quetiapine and olanzapine prolong QT only modestly (escitalopram by about 7 msec at 20 mg), and for metronidazole the evidence is case reports while fluoxetine's effect is marginal, so treat all of those as a reason to check rather than a reason to expect it.

The SSRI with a genuinely QT-driven dose restriction is CITALOPRAM, not escitalopram.

A seizure happens when excitation outruns inhibition. Several of these drugs shift that balance a little: bupropion by raising dopamine and norepinephrine, the antipsychotics by blocking dopamine, the tricyclics through multiple receptors, methylphenidate by raising catecholamines, and the fluoroquinolones by blocking GABA-A directly.

Bupropion is the one that matters most, which is why it is in its own group. Both shift the balance slightly. After each beat the ventricle has to repolarize, meaning reset its electrical charge, before it can beat again. Potassium leaving the cell through the hERG channel is what does that. These drugs block hERG, so repolarization drags out. That dragged-out reset is what a long QT measures, and a beat firing during that stretched window can tip the rhythm into torsades de pointes.

They do not all carry the same weight. Ondansetron, methadone, prochlorperazine, chlorpromazine, haloperidol, amitriptyline, the fluoroquinolones and the macrolides, Bactrim, and the antiarrhythmics amiodarone and procainamide are the established ones. Loperamide belongs here only at HIGHER THAN RECOMMENDED doses, which is what its boxed warning is about. For the antiarrhythmics the QT effect IS the mechanism, not a side effect, which is why a class IA or class III drug can treat an arrhythmia and cause torsades with the same action. Stopping a bleed takes two steps. Platelets clump together to form a plug, then a mesh of fibrin locks that plug in place. These drugs attack different steps.

Anticoagulants stop the fibrin mesh. Antiplatelets stop the plug. NSAIDs do two things at once by blocking COX-1: they weaken platelets AND strip the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, so you get worse clotting and a surface more likely to bleed. SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need in order to clump.

Combine any two and the risk compounds. Some of these pairs are closer to additive than multiplied, but none of them are safe to stack without watching for it.

The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

CYCLOSPORINE belongs to the first mechanism rather than the third: its acute nephrotoxicity is AFFERENT arteriolar vasoconstriction, the same vessel an NSAID narrows, which is why cyclosporine plus an NSAID is worse than simply additive.

Gentamicin and vancomycin skip all of that and injure the tubule itself, so they add to any of the three. IV acyclovir is a third kind: it crystallizes inside the tubule when the urine is concentrated, which makes it a hydration problem rather than a dose problem, and it applies to the IV route only.

An NSAID blocks the prostaglandins, so the afferent arteriole narrows and less blood gets in. An ACE inhibitor or ARB blocks angiotensin II, so the efferent arteriole relaxes open and pressure escapes. A diuretic drops the volume arriving at both. Take all three and filtration pressure collapses.

Antihypertensives and diuretics rely partly on prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation and renal sodium handling. NSAIDs block prostaglandin synthesis, so the BP drug works less well and sodium is retained.

After each beat the ventricle has to repolarize, meaning reset its electrical charge, before it can beat again. Potassium leaving the cell through the hERG channel is what does that. These drugs block hERG, so repolarization drags out. That dragged-out reset is what a long QT measures, and a beat firing during that stretched window can tip the rhythm into torsades de pointes.

NSAIDs remove the prostaglandins that protect gastric mucosa. Steroids impair mucosal healing and mask the pain that would warn you. SSRIs add impaired platelet function on top.

Stopping a bleed takes two steps. Platelets clump together to form a plug, then a mesh of fibrin locks that plug in place. These drugs attack different steps.

Anticoagulants stop the fibrin mesh. Antiplatelets stop the plug. NSAIDs do two things at once by blocking COX-1: they weaken platelets AND strip the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, so you get worse clotting and a surface more likely to bleed. SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need in order to clump.

Combine any two and the risk compounds. Some of these pairs are closer to additive than multiplied, but none of them are safe to stack without watching for it.

After each beat the ventricle has to repolarize, meaning reset its electrical charge, before it can beat again. Potassium leaving the cell through the hERG channel is what does that. Stopping a bleed takes two steps. Platelets clump together to form a plug, then a mesh of fibrin locks that plug in place. These drugs attack different steps.

Anticoagulants stop the fibrin mesh. Antiplatelets stop the plug. NSAIDs do two things at once by blocking COX-1: they weaken platelets AND strip the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, so you get worse clotting and a surface more likely to bleed. SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need in order to clump.

Combine any two and the risk compounds. Some of these pairs are closer to additive than multiplied, but none of them are safe to stack without watching for it.

ACE inhibitors and ARBs remove aldosterone, so the kidney stops dumping K⁺. Trimethoprim blocks the distal tubule sodium channel directly, which is structurally how amiloride works. Heparin and enoxaparin suppress aldosterone synthesis in the adrenal gland, independent of their anticoagulant effect.

The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

CYCLOSPORINE belongs to the first mechanism rather than the third: its acute nephrotoxicity is AFFERENT arteriolar vasoconstriction, the same vessel an NSAID narrows, which is why cyclosporine plus an NSAID is worse than simply additive.

Gentamicin and vancomycin skip all of that and injure the tubule itself, so they add to any of the three. IV acyclovir is a third kind: it crystallizes inside the tubule when the urine is concentrated, which makes it a hydration problem rather than a dose problem, and it applies to the IV route only.

An NSAID blocks the prostaglandins, so the afferent arteriole narrows and less blood gets in. An ACE inhibitor or ARB blocks angiotensin II, so the efferent arteriole relaxes open and pressure escapes. A diuretic drops the volume arriving at both. Take all three and filtration pressure collapses.

CYCLOSPORINE belongs to the first mechanism rather than the third: its acute nephrotoxicity is AFFERENT arteriolar vasoconstriction, the same vessel an NSAID narrows, which is why cyclosporine plus an NSAID is worse than simply additive.

Gentamicin and vancomycin skip all of that and injure the tubule itself, so they add to any of the three. IV acyclovir is a third kind: it crystallizes inside the tubule when the urine is concentrated, which makes it a hydration problem rather than a dose problem, and it applies to the IV route only.

Take all three and filtration pressure collapses. Minimal additive effect at cardioprotective doses.

Steroids drive gluconeogenesis and reduce peripheral glucose uptake, so insulin requirements rise, sometimes steeply. Beta blockers do something different and more dangerous: they mask the adrenergic warning signs of hypoglycemia (tremor, tachycardia) while sweating still comes through.

Epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine and dobutamine all work through adrenergic receptors. A beta blocker already occupying those receptors reduces the response, so the usual dose does less than expected. With epinephrine the picture is worse: beta blockade leaves alpha effects unopposed, which can produce severe hypertension with reflex bradycardia. Atenolol and metoprolol are CARDIOSELECTIVE, so this pairing is common and deliberate: beta blockers reduce mortality after MI and in heart failure, and COPD is not a reason to withhold them. Selectivity is dose-dependent, so at high doses watch for wheeze, but do not treat the combination as an error.

Each of these blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. One drug gives you a dry mouth. Two or three give you the full picture: blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, blocked sweating so heat cannot be shed, and in older adults an acute confusion that gets charted as dementia or a UTI rather than as the drugs.

The clinical point is that total load matters, not any single drug. This is what the Beers criteria are built around, and it is the most common reversible cause of delirium in a hospitalized older adult.

The three that most often go uncounted are DIPHENHYDRAMINE (in sleep aids and cold remedies the patient does not call medication), BENZTROPINE (given to treat the side effects of an antipsychotic that is itself anticholinergic), and PROMETHAZINE. Add any two and an older adult is at real risk.

Too much serotonin at the synapse. The SSRIs and SNRIs here (fluoxetine, sertraline, escitalopram, venlafaxine, duloxetine) raise it directly by blocking its reuptake. Amitriptyline does the same, alongside norepinephrine. Methadone and buspirone contribute weakly.

Ondansetron and metoclopramide are a different case. They BLOCK serotonin receptors rather than raising serotonin, and the link to serotonin syndrome rests on case reports with no established mechanism. Treat them as a reason to look, not a reason to expect it. Weaker on both sides. A reason to watch, not to expect it.

A seizure happens when excitation outruns inhibition. Several of these drugs shift that balance a little: bupropion by raising dopamine and norepinephrine, the antipsychotics by blocking dopamine, the tricyclics through multiple receptors, methylphenidate by raising catecholamines, and the fluoroquinolones by blocking GABA-A directly.

One of them alone rarely causes a seizure in a patient with no risk factors. Stacked, or added to withdrawal, head injury, hyponatremia, an eating disorder or a prior seizure, the margin gets thin. Bupropion is the one that matters most, which is why it is in its own group. Weak. Flagged through the fluoroquinolone link rather than on its own.

Opioids blunt the brainstem's response to rising CO₂. Benzodiazepines amplify GABA. Gabapentinoids damp excitatory transmission. Stacked, the drive to breathe can disappear while the patient simply looks asleep. Additive sedation, and a frequent deliberate pairing in neuropathic pain. Expect it and monitor rather than treat it as an error.

A seizure happens when excitation outruns inhibition. Several of these drugs shift that balance a little: bupropion by raising dopamine and norepinephrine, the antipsychotics by blocking dopamine, the tricyclics through multiple receptors, methylphenidate by raising catecholamines, and the fluoroquinolones by blocking GABA-A directly.

One of them alone rarely causes a seizure in a patient with no risk factors. Stacked, or added to withdrawal, head injury, hyponatremia, an eating disorder or a prior seizure, the margin gets thin. Bupropion is the one that matters most, which is why it is in its own group. Weak. Flagged through the fluoroquinolone link rather than on its own.

Methylphenidate raises synaptic norepinephrine, which raises heart rate and blood pressure. That works directly against every antihypertensive, and it adds to anything else that is already adrenergic.

Scoped to methylphenidate on purpose. DOBUTAMINE is deliberately NOT here: it is a beta-1 inotrope and its label says systemic vascular resistance is usually DECREASED, so it does not oppose an antihypertensive. Flagging it against a heart failure patient's own medication list would be backwards.
Amlodipine weakly inhibits CYP3A4 → simvastatin is capped at 20 mg with it.

Antibiotics kill the colonic flora that keeps Clostridioides difficile suppressed. The organism overgrows and releases toxin, which inflames the colon. It can start during therapy or up to two months after it stops.

The trap is the treatment. An ANTIMOTILITY drug such as loperamide or diphenoxylate slows the bowel and TRAPS the toxin against the mucosa, which turns colitis into ileus and toxic megacolon. Diarrhea in a patient on or recently off an antibiotic is a stool test and a phone call, never an antidiarrheal. Note that a stool SOFTENER like docusate is a different drug class and does not carry this risk. Acid suppression raises the risk further by removing the gastric barrier. Acid suppression raises C. difficile risk on top of the antibiotic, because stomach acid is part of the barrier. Common and often appropriate, so the action is to ask whether the acid suppression is still indicated, not to stop the antibiotic.

Antihypertensives and diuretics rely partly on prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation and renal sodium handling. NSAIDs block prostaglandin synthesis, so the BP drug works less well and sodium is retained. Cardioprotective aspirin at 81 mg does not meaningfully blunt an antihypertensive, and the combination is standard in coronary disease. The blunting effect belongs to anti-inflammatory doses.

Stopping a bleed takes two steps. Platelets clump together to form a plug, then a mesh of fibrin locks that plug in place. These drugs attack different steps.

Anticoagulants stop the fibrin mesh. Antiplatelets stop the plug. NSAIDs do two things at once by blocking COX-1: they weaken platelets AND strip the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, so you get worse clotting and a surface more likely to bleed. SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need in order to clump.

Combine any two and the risk compounds. Some of these pairs are closer to additive than multiplied, but none of them are safe to stack without watching for it. Additive salicylate and COX effect; also additive tinnitus risk as a marker of salicylate excess.

The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

CYCLOSPORINE belongs to the first mechanism rather than the third: its acute nephrotoxicity is AFFERENT arteriolar vasoconstriction, the same vessel an NSAID narrows, which is why cyclosporine plus an NSAID is worse than simply additive.

Gentamicin and vancomycin skip all of that and injure the tubule itself, so they add to any of the three. IV acyclovir is a third kind: it crystallizes inside the tubule when the urine is concentrated, which makes it a hydration problem rather than a dose problem, and it applies to the IV route only.

An NSAID blocks the prostaglandins, so the afferent arteriole narrows and less blood gets in. An ACE inhibitor or ARB blocks angiotensin II, so the efferent arteriole relaxes open and pressure escapes. A diuretic drops the volume arriving at both. Take all three and filtration pressure collapses. Same: at 81 mg this is routine. At analgesic doses treat it as an NSAID.

The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

CYCLOSPORINE belongs to the first mechanism rather than the third: its acute nephrotoxicity is AFFERENT arteriolar vasoconstriction, the same vessel an NSAID narrows, which is why cyclosporine plus an NSAID is worse than simply additive.

Gentamicin and vancomycin skip all of that and injure the tubule itself, so they add to any of the three. IV acyclovir is a third kind: it crystallizes inside the tubule when the urine is concentrated, which makes it a hydration problem rather than a dose problem, and it applies to the IV route only.

An NSAID blocks the prostaglandins, so the afferent arteriole narrows and less blood gets in. An ACE inhibitor or ARB blocks angiotensin II, so the efferent arteriole relaxes open and pressure escapes. A diuretic drops the volume arriving at both. Take all three and filtration pressure collapses. Same: at 81 mg this is routine. At analgesic doses treat it as an NSAID.

Nitroglycerin and hydralazine drop pressure fast. Added to a patient already on a beta blocker, a diuretic or a RAAS blocker, the fall can be abrupt rather than gradual.

This rule is deliberately limited to those two rapid vasodilators. Routine oral combination therapy, such as amlodipine with lisinopril, is standard practice and is NOT flagged here.

Steroids drive gluconeogenesis and reduce peripheral glucose uptake, so insulin requirements rise, sometimes steeply. Beta blockers do something different and more dangerous: they mask the adrenergic warning signs of hypoglycemia (tremor, tachycardia) while sweating still comes through.

Epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine and dobutamine all work through adrenergic receptors. A beta blocker already occupying those receptors reduces the response, so the usual dose does less than expected. With epinephrine the picture is worse: beta blockade leaves alpha effects unopposed, which can produce severe hypertension with reflex bradycardia. Atenolol and metoprolol are CARDIOSELECTIVE, so this pairing is common and deliberate: beta blockers reduce mortality after MI and in heart failure, and COPD is not a reason to withhold them. Selectivity is dose-dependent, so at high doses watch for wheeze, but do not treat the combination as an error.

Statins, fibrates and niacin each injure muscle on their own, and together the risk climbs. Muscle pain and weakness are the warning. Rhabdomyolysis is the endpoint: muscle breaking down fast enough to damage the kidneys.

Why this is moderate and not high: the fibrate behind the serious cases is GEMFIBROZIL, which slows how fast the body clears a statin, so the statin builds up. Fenofibrate does not do that, which is exactly why it is the fibrate you pair with a statin. Gemfibrozil is not in this set.

How statins injure muscle at all is still unsettled. The leading explanation is that the pathway they block also supplies coenzyme Q10 to muscle.

Each of these blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. One drug gives you a dry mouth. Two or three give you the full picture: blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, blocked sweating so heat cannot be shed, and in older adults an acute confusion that gets charted as dementia or a UTI rather than as the drugs.

The clinical point is that total load matters, not any single drug. This is what the Beers criteria are built around, and it is the most common reversible cause of delirium in a hospitalized older adult.

The three that most often go uncounted are DIPHENHYDRAMINE (in sleep aids and cold remedies the patient does not call medication), BENZTROPINE (given to treat the side effects of an antipsychotic that is itself anticholinergic), and PROMETHAZINE. Add any two and an older adult is at real risk.

Antibiotics kill the colonic flora that keeps Clostridioides difficile suppressed. The organism overgrows and releases toxin, which inflames the colon. It can start during therapy or up to two months after it stops.

The trap is the treatment. An ANTIMOTILITY drug such as loperamide or diphenoxylate slows the bowel and TRAPS the toxin against the mucosa, which turns colitis into ileus and toxic megacolon. Diarrhea in a patient on or recently off an antibiotic is a stool test and a phone call, never an antidiarrheal. Note that a stool SOFTENER like docusate is a different drug class and does not carry this risk. Acid suppression raises the risk further by removing the gastric barrier. Acid suppression raises C. difficile risk on top of the antibiotic, because stomach acid is part of the barrier. Common and often appropriate, so the action is to ask whether the acid suppression is still indicated, not to stop the antibiotic.
The same two mechanisms, more weakly. Worth a level if the patient is already near the top of the range.

The hair cells of the cochlea and the vestibular apparatus do not regenerate. Aminoglycosides accumulate in them and kill them. Loop diuretics damage the same structures through the ion pump in the inner ear, and high-dose IV erythromycin and vancomycin add to it.

That is the asymmetry worth holding on to: the kidney injury these drugs cause is usually reversible, and the hearing loss usually is not. So a rising creatinine is a reason to adjust, while tinnitus is a reason to stop and call. Weaker on both sides. Worth noting in a patient already getting high-dose IV vancomycin with aggressive diuresis, and not otherwise.

Divalent and trivalent cations chelate fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines in the gut, forming a complex that is never absorbed. Sevelamer is a polymer that binds far more than phosphate. Raising gastric pH changes absorption of drugs that need acid.

Stopping a bleed takes two steps. Platelets clump together to form a plug, then a mesh of fibrin locks that plug in place. These drugs attack different steps.

Anticoagulants stop the fibrin mesh. Antiplatelets stop the plug. NSAIDs do two things at once by blocking COX-1: they weaken platelets AND strip the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, so you get worse clotting and a surface more likely to bleed. SSRIs and SNRIs drain the serotonin platelets need in order to clump.

Stopping a bleed takes two steps. Platelets clump together to form a plug, then a mesh of fibrin locks that plug in place. These drugs attack different steps.

The hair cells of the cochlea and the vestibular apparatus do not regenerate. Aminoglycosides accumulate in them and kill them. Loop diuretics damage the same structures through the ion pump in the inner ear, and high-dose IV erythromycin and vancomycin add to it.

That is the asymmetry worth holding on to: the kidney injury these drugs cause is usually reversible, and the hearing loss usually is not. So a rising creatinine is a reason to adjust, while tinnitus is a reason to stop and call. Weaker on both sides. Worth noting in a patient already getting high-dose IV vancomycin with aggressive diuresis, and not otherwise.

The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

CYCLOSPORINE belongs to the first mechanism rather than the third: its acute nephrotoxicity is AFFERENT arteriolar vasoconstriction, the same vessel an NSAID narrows, which is why cyclosporine plus an NSAID is worse than simply additive.

Gentamicin and vancomycin skip all of that and injure the tubule itself, so they add to any of the three. IV acyclovir is a third kind: it crystallizes inside the tubule when the urine is concentrated, which makes it a hydration problem rather than a dose problem, and it applies to the IV route only.

An NSAID blocks the prostaglandins, so the afferent arteriole narrows and less blood gets in. An ACE inhibitor or ARB blocks angiotensin II, so the efferent arteriole relaxes open and pressure escapes. A diuretic drops the volume arriving at both. Take all three and filtration pressure collapses. An ACE inhibitor or ARB WITH a loop diuretic is guideline-directed therapy in heart failure, not an error. It becomes the triple whammy only when an NSAID joins. Monitor creatinine; do not treat the pair itself as a problem.

Nitroglycerin and hydralazine drop pressure fast. Added to a patient already on a beta blocker, a diuretic or a RAAS blocker, the fall can be abrupt rather than gradual.

This rule is deliberately limited to those two rapid vasodilators. Routine oral combination therapy, such as amlodipine with lisinopril, is standard practice and is NOT flagged here.

A seizure happens when excitation outruns inhibition. Several of these drugs shift that balance a little: bupropion by raising dopamine and norepinephrine, the antipsychotics by blocking dopamine, the tricyclics through multiple receptors, methylphenidate by raising catecholamines, and the fluoroquinolones by blocking GABA-A directly.

One of them alone rarely causes a seizure in a patient with no risk factors. Stacked, or added to withdrawal, head injury, hyponatremia, an eating disorder or a prior seizure, the margin gets thin. Bupropion is the one that matters most, which is why it is in its own group. Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold and the NSAID contributes little on its own. Noted for completeness.
Same prodrug problem as fluoxetine: 2D6 blocked → codeine never becomes morphine → no analgesia.
Same: abrupt benzodiazepine withdrawal while bupropion continues lowers the seizure threshold from both directions. Taper.
Two 2D6 inhibitors, plus additive lowering of the seizure threshold.

Giving these together is fine. The hazard is STOPPING the lorazepam abruptly: benzodiazepines RAISE the seizure threshold, so abrupt withdrawal of one is an explicit bupropion contraindication. Same for diazepam and alprazolam. Taper the benzodiazepine, and taper it more carefully because bupropion is on board.
Bupropion is a potent CYP2D6 inhibitor too. Its label names beta blockers (e.g. metoprolol) and advises considering a dose reduction.

Too much serotonin at the synapse. The SSRIs and SNRIs here (fluoxetine, sertraline, escitalopram, venlafaxine, duloxetine) raise it directly by blocking its reuptake. Amitriptyline does the same, alongside norepinephrine. Methadone and buspirone contribute weakly.

Ondansetron and metoclopramide are a different case. They BLOCK serotonin receptors rather than raising serotonin, and the link to serotonin syndrome rests on case reports with no established mechanism. Treat them as a reason to look, not a reason to expect it. One strong serotonergic drug plus a weak contributor. Monitor; do not assume.

The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

CYCLOSPORINE belongs to the first mechanism rather than the third: its acute nephrotoxicity is AFFERENT arteriolar vasoconstriction, the same vessel an NSAID narrows, which is why cyclosporine plus an NSAID is worse than simply additive.

Gentamicin and vancomycin skip all of that and injure the tubule itself, so they add to any of the three. IV acyclovir is a third kind: it crystallizes inside the tubule when the urine is concentrated, which makes it a hydration problem rather than a dose problem, and it applies to the IV route only.

An NSAID blocks the prostaglandins, so the afferent arteriole narrows and less blood gets in. An ACE inhibitor or ARB blocks angiotensin II, so the efferent arteriole relaxes open and pressure escapes. A diuretic drops the volume arriving at both. Take all three and filtration pressure collapses. An ACE inhibitor or ARB WITH a loop diuretic is guideline-directed therapy in heart failure, not an error. It becomes the triple whammy only when an NSAID joins. Monitor creatinine; do not treat the pair itself as a problem.

Antibiotics kill the colonic flora that keeps Clostridioides difficile suppressed. The organism overgrows and releases toxin, which inflames the colon. It can start during therapy or up to two months after it stops.

The trap is the treatment. An ANTIMOTILITY drug such as loperamide or diphenoxylate slows the bowel and TRAPS the toxin against the mucosa, which turns colitis into ileus and toxic megacolon. Diarrhea in a patient on or recently off an antibiotic is a stool test and a phone call, never an antidiarrheal. Note that a stool SOFTENER like docusate is a different drug class and does not carry this risk. Acid suppression raises the risk further by removing the gastric barrier. Acid suppression raises C. difficile risk on top of the antibiotic, because stomach acid is part of the barrier. Common and often appropriate, so the action is to ask whether the acid suppression is still indicated, not to stop the antibiotic.

A seizure happens when excitation outruns inhibition. Several of these drugs shift that balance a little: bupropion by raising dopamine and norepinephrine, the antipsychotics by blocking dopamine, the tricyclics through multiple receptors, methylphenidate by raising catecholamines, and the fluoroquinolones by blocking GABA-A directly.

One of them alone rarely causes a seizure in a patient with no risk factors. Stacked, or added to withdrawal, head injury, hyponatremia, an eating disorder or a prior seizure, the margin gets thin. Bupropion is the one that matters most, which is why it is in its own group. Weak. Flagged through the fluoroquinolone link rather than on its own.

Each of these blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. One drug gives you a dry mouth. Two or three give you the full picture: blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, blocked sweating so heat cannot be shed, and in older adults an acute confusion that gets charted as dementia or a UTI rather than as the drugs.

The clinical point is that total load matters, not any single drug. This is what the Beers criteria are built around, and it is the most common reversible cause of delirium in a hospitalized older adult.

The three that most often go uncounted are DIPHENHYDRAMINE (in sleep aids and cold remedies the patient does not call medication), BENZTROPINE (given to treat the side effects of an antipsychotic that is itself anticholinergic), and PROMETHAZINE. Add any two and an older adult is at real risk.

Antibiotics kill the colonic flora that keeps Clostridioides difficile suppressed. The organism overgrows and releases toxin, which inflames the colon. It can start during therapy or up to two months after it stops.

The trap is the treatment. An ANTIMOTILITY drug such as loperamide or diphenoxylate slows the bowel and TRAPS the toxin against the mucosa, which turns colitis into ileus and toxic megacolon. Diarrhea in a patient on or recently off an antibiotic is a stool test and a phone call, never an antidiarrheal. Note that a stool SOFTENER like docusate is a different drug class and does not carry this risk. Acid suppression raises the risk further by removing the gastric barrier. Acid suppression raises C. difficile risk on top of the antibiotic, because stomach acid is part of the barrier. Common and often appropriate, so the action is to ask whether the acid suppression is still indicated, not to stop the antibiotic.

Codeine is a prodrug needing CYP2D6 to become morphine. Fluoxetine blocks that conversion → no analgesia, and the patient is told their pain medication 'doesn't work.'

Opioids blunt the brainstem's response to rising CO₂. Benzodiazepines amplify GABA. Gabapentinoids damp excitatory transmission. Stacked, the drive to breathe can disappear while the patient simply looks asleep. Common and appropriate, since opioids themselves cause nausea. The caution is additive sedation, not that the pair is wrong.

A seizure happens when excitation outruns inhibition. Several of these drugs shift that balance a little: bupropion by raising dopamine and norepinephrine, the antipsychotics by blocking dopamine, the tricyclics through multiple receptors, methylphenidate by raising catecholamines, and the fluoroquinolones by blocking GABA-A directly.

One of them alone rarely causes a seizure in a patient with no risk factors. Stacked, or added to withdrawal, head injury, hyponatremia, an eating disorder or a prior seizure, the margin gets thin. Bupropion is the one that matters most, which is why it is in its own group. Both shift the balance slightly. Worth noticing, and worth acting on only if the patient has another risk factor: a seizure history, withdrawal, head injury, hyponatremia or an eating disorder.

Statins, fibrates and niacin each injure muscle on their own, and together the risk climbs. Muscle pain and weakness are the warning. Rhabdomyolysis is the endpoint: muscle breaking down fast enough to damage the kidneys.

Why this is moderate and not high: the fibrate behind the serious cases is GEMFIBROZIL, which slows how fast the body clears a statin, so the statin builds up. Fenofibrate does not do that, which is exactly why it is the fibrate you pair with a statin. Gemfibrozil is not in this set.

How statins injure muscle at all is still unsettled. The leading explanation is that the pathway they block also supplies coenzyme Q10 to muscle.

Nitroglycerin and hydralazine drop pressure fast. Added to a patient already on a beta blocker, a diuretic or a RAAS blocker, the fall can be abrupt rather than gradual.

This rule is deliberately limited to those two rapid vasodilators. Routine oral combination therapy, such as amlodipine with lisinopril, is standard practice and is NOT flagged here.

Each of these blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. One drug gives you a dry mouth. Two or three give you the full picture: blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, blocked sweating so heat cannot be shed, and in older adults an acute confusion that gets charted as dementia or a UTI rather than as the drugs.

The clinical point is that total load matters, not any single drug. This is what the Beers criteria are built around, and it is the most common reversible cause of delirium in a hospitalized older adult.

The three that most often go uncounted are DIPHENHYDRAMINE (in sleep aids and cold remedies the patient does not call medication), BENZTROPINE (given to treat the side effects of an antipsychotic that is itself anticholinergic), and PROMETHAZINE. Add any two and an older adult is at real risk.

A seizure happens when excitation outruns inhibition. Several of these drugs shift that balance a little: bupropion by raising dopamine and norepinephrine, the antipsychotics by blocking dopamine, the tricyclics through multiple receptors, methylphenidate by raising catecholamines, and the fluoroquinolones by blocking GABA-A directly.

One of them alone rarely causes a seizure in a patient with no risk factors. Stacked, or added to withdrawal, head injury, hyponatremia, an eating disorder or a prior seizure, the margin gets thin. Bupropion is the one that matters most, which is why it is in its own group. Overlapping membership; the fluoroquinolone is already counted in the contributes group.

Each of these blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. One drug gives you a dry mouth. Two or three give you the full picture: blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, blocked sweating so heat cannot be shed, and in older adults an acute confusion that gets charted as dementia or a UTI rather than as the drugs.

The clinical point is that total load matters, not any single drug. This is what the Beers criteria are built around, and it is the most common reversible cause of delirium in a hospitalized older adult.

The three that most often go uncounted are DIPHENHYDRAMINE (in sleep aids and cold remedies the patient does not call medication), BENZTROPINE (given to treat the side effects of an antipsychotic that is itself anticholinergic), and PROMETHAZINE. Add any two and an older adult is at real risk.

Epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine and dobutamine all work through adrenergic receptors. A beta blocker already occupying those receptors reduces the response, so the usual dose does less than expected. With epinephrine the picture is worse: beta blockade leaves alpha effects unopposed, which can produce severe hypertension with reflex bradycardia. Additive adrenergic effect on heart rate, tremor and potassium. Common in a patient treated for both shock and bronchospasm.

The glomerulus filters by pressure, and it holds that pressure with two vessels. Prostaglandins dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood in. Angiotensin II constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, the one carrying blood out. Wide inlet, narrow outlet: pressure builds between them, and that pressure is what pushes filtrate across.

CYCLOSPORINE belongs to the first mechanism rather than the third: its acute nephrotoxicity is AFFERENT arteriolar vasoconstriction, the same vessel an NSAID narrows, which is why cyclosporine plus an NSAID is worse than simply additive.

Gentamicin and vancomycin skip all of that and injure the tubule itself, so they add to any of the three. IV acyclovir is a third kind: it crystallizes inside the tubule when the urine is concentrated, which makes it a hydration problem rather than a dose problem, and it applies to the IV route only.

An NSAID blocks the prostaglandins, so the afferent arteriole narrows and less blood gets in. An ACE inhibitor or ARB blocks angiotensin II, so the efferent arteriole relaxes open and pressure escapes. A diuretic drops the volume arriving at both. Take all three and filtration pressure collapses. An ACE inhibitor or ARB WITH a loop diuretic is guideline-directed therapy in heart failure, not an error. It becomes the triple whammy only when an NSAID joins. Monitor creatinine; do not treat the pair itself as a problem.

Nitroglycerin and hydralazine drop pressure fast. Added to a patient already on a beta blocker, a diuretic or a RAAS blocker, the fall can be abrupt rather than gradual.

This rule is deliberately limited to those two rapid vasodilators. Routine oral combination therapy, such as amlodipine with lisinopril, is standard practice and is NOT flagged here.

Steroids drive gluconeogenesis and reduce peripheral glucose uptake, so insulin requirements rise, sometimes steeply. Beta blockers do something different and more dangerous: they mask the adrenergic warning signs of hypoglycemia (tremor, tachycardia) while sweating still comes through. Additive glucose lowering. Monitor more often rather than treating it as an error.

Antibiotics kill the colonic flora that keeps Clostridioides difficile suppressed. The organism overgrows and releases toxin, which inflames the colon. It can start during therapy or up to two months after it stops.

The trap is the treatment. An ANTIMOTILITY drug such as loperamide or diphenoxylate slows the bowel and TRAPS the toxin against the mucosa, which turns colitis into ileus and toxic megacolon. Diarrhea in a patient on or recently off an antibiotic is a stool test and a phone call, never an antidiarrheal. Note that a stool SOFTENER like docusate is a different drug class and does not carry this risk. Acid suppression raises the risk further by removing the gastric barrier. Acid suppression raises C. difficile risk on top of the antibiotic, because stomach acid is part of the barrier. Common and often appropriate, so the action is to ask whether the acid suppression is still indicated, not to stop the antibiotic.

Some drugs need an acidic stomach to dissolve or to be absorbed. Raise the pH with a proton pump inhibitor or an H2 blocker and less of the drug gets in, so the patient takes it faithfully and gets a reduced effect.

Scoped deliberately to calcium carbonate and iron, where the effect is documented and clinically visible. SUCRALFATE is NOT here: although it polymerizes in acid in vitro, its label permits antacids with only a 30-minute separation and it is routinely co-prescribed with an H2 blocker or a PPI. Sucralfate's real interaction runs the other way, binding other drugs in the gut.

Statins, fibrates and niacin each injure muscle on their own, and together the risk climbs. Muscle pain and weakness are the warning. Rhabdomyolysis is the endpoint: muscle breaking down fast enough to damage the kidneys.

Why this is moderate and not high: the fibrate behind the serious cases is GEMFIBROZIL, which slows how fast the body clears a statin, so the statin builds up. Fenofibrate does not do that, which is exactly why it is the fibrate you pair with a statin. Gemfibrozil is not in this set.

How statins injure muscle at all is still unsettled. The leading explanation is that the pathway they block also supplies coenzyme Q10 to muscle.
